title: Watch Stéphane Cuenat’s TEDx talk
text:
The Answer You Can’t Check
The essay I wrote at the time of the talk.
AI is extraordinary—until it reaches the edge of what we know. And there, the most dangerous thing it can hand you is a convincing answer with nothing left to check it against.
A few months ago I was working on a problem in machine learning: deriving the upper and lower bounds of a classifier—the mathematical limits of how well it can possibly perform. It’s slow, careful work, the kind where a single wrong assumption quietly invalidates everything built on top of it.
I used an AI model to help. And it did help—a lot. It also nearly cost me weeks. I want to be honest about that, because I suspect many people are quietly having the same experience and not saying it out loud.
At one point it handed me a set of conjectures that were clean, well-motivated, and elegantly argued. They looked exactly like the kind of result the literature would produce. I started building on them. It was only later, checking by hand, that I realized they were subtly false—the form of a proof without the substance.
That experience crystallized something I’ve come to believe is the real risk of these tools. It isn’t the hallucination you catch. A claim that’s obviously wrong is harmless; you discard it and move on. The dangerous failure mode is the plausible conjecture you don’t catch—the answer that’s credible enough to believe and false enough to lead you off a cliff. And at the frontier, where research actually lives, there is often nothing left to check it against. That, far more than unreliability, is the problem I want to talk about.

Where the trouble starts
To understand why this happens, it helps to be precise about what these systems are extraordinarily good at, and where they quietly break.
Large models are brilliant at recombining what already exists. Inside the space of everything they’ve seen—every paper, every proof, every pattern—they interpolate beautifully. Ask them for something that lives within that space, and they’ll produce it faster and more fluently than any human.
The trouble starts at the edges. At extrapolation—the genuinely new—they don’t stop. They fill the gap with something that looks like the answer the existing literature would have produced. In most everyday tasks that’s fine, because the answer really does live inside the known space. But research, by definition, lives at the frontier—the business of reaching what doesn’t exist yet. And whether or not a model can occasionally reach that far, it has no way to tell a genuine reach from a confident guess. To the system, both feel identical.
The model doesn’t know it has crossed from interpolation into invention. It has no internal signal that says here, I am guessing. It produces the plausible artifact with the same confidence it produces a correct one.


The missing oracle
There’s a deeper reason this is so hard to defend against, and it has nothing to do with the model being unreliable. It’s about verification.
When you work on a known problem, you have an oracle. You can check the answer against an established result, a textbook, a dataset, a colleague who has done it before. The plausible-but-wrong answer gets caught because there’s ground truth to catch it.
At the frontier, that oracle is gone. There is no established result, because the whole point is that the result is new. So when a system hands you a clean conjecture about something nobody has settled, what external truth do you check it against? Its internal consistency isn’t enough—a wrong idea can be perfectly self-consistent. That’s precisely what made my false conjectures so seductive: they hung together. They just weren’t true.
This is the question I keep coming back to whenever someone announces that an AI has “discovered” something new. The interesting test of a discovery isn’t whether the model produced it, or even whether it’s elegant. It’s whether the discovery makes a prediction you can take back to the world and be proven wrong on. A model concise enough to generate a falsifiable experiment has an external oracle—reality itself. That’s the line between genuine discovery and a very clever fit. Without it, you have internal consistency dressed up as insight.


The compass at the frontier
It would be easy to read all of this as an argument that AI can’t do real science. It isn’t—I use these tools every day, and they make me faster and sharper. And I think betting against their reach is a mistake. These systems can sometimes arrive at genuinely novel points, and the line between sophisticated recombination and true extrapolation is blurrier than the skeptics like to admit. That line will keep moving, and I won’t bet against it.
The harder, more durable gap is somewhere else. There are actually two halves to the frontier problem, and they belong together. The missing oracle is why you can’t check the answer once you have it. But there is a question that comes before that one: how do you know where to look at all? At the frontier there is no gradient to follow—no signal that says this direction is worth pursuing, or this elegant construct is actually true. What fills that gap, for a human, is intuition.
I mean something specific, not mystical. Mathematicians routinely sense that a result is true long before they can prove it, and that conviction is what tells them where to spend the next six months. Physicists feel that an equation is “too ugly to be right.” That intuition isn’t magic; it’s a different and far richer kind of training—built from embodied experience, from transfer across unrelated domains, from years of being wrong in instructive ways. And crucially, it comes with calibrated doubt: a person at the edge of their knowledge usually knows when they’re guessing. Models can be made to express uncertainty too—but in my experience, it is precisely on the novel, plausible construct that this signal fails. The conjectures that nearly fooled me did not arrive flagged as guesses. They arrived looking like results.
So the asymmetry I find genuinely hopeful isn’t that machines can’t reach the new. It’s that reaching the new—where nothing can be checked—still depends on a sense of direction the model doesn’t have: the judgment to choose which unknown is worth chasing, and the instinct to feel when a beautiful answer is hollow. The impossible has been human territory not because we compute our way there, but because we carry a compass for it.
That’s not a limitation waiting to be patched in the next model generation. It’s a description of two different kinds of work. One is recombination—and maybe even genuine reach—at superhuman speed. The other is knowing where to point it, and knowing when you’ve actually arrived.
So the posture I’ve landed on is simple, maybe even a little old-fashioned. For me, AI is a tool—and only a tool. Not a replacement for judgment, for expertise, or for the slow work of actually understanding a problem. So I challenge every output, because the convincing ones are the dangerous ones, and I try to never take the output as truth. Used with that in mind, it brings a lot. Used blindly, it’s a rendez-vous to fail. The rest—deciding what’s worth reaching for, and recognizing when you’ve actually arrived—is the part no model can do for me. That part I keep for myself.
Keep the tool. Keep your head too.
I made a version of this case on a TEDx stage—“The Impossible: A Springboard for Humans, a Frontier for AI.” If the argument here interests you, the talk goes a little further: watch it on YouTube.

Questions and counter-arguments about the talk are welcome: find me on LinkedIn.

title: It Must Be Simpler Than This
text:
Position paper, November 2026. A provocative paper, on purpose. A short paper with a thesis, a measure, two small worked examples and predictions that could prove it wrong. It gathers one idea that runs, mostly unnamed, through every post on this site since September, from dashboards and agents to black holes. Figures are my own; the numbers in Figures 1 and 2 are computed by figs.py and stored in results.json.
Abstract. We call a system complex when describing it takes a long time. I argue that this length is mostly a property of the description, not of the system. Formally, the apparent complexity A(x) of a thing is the length of the description we actually use; its intrinsic complexity is the length of the shortest description that would regenerate it, a rule plus what the rule leaves out, K(x) \lesssim L(G) + L(x \mid G). The gap A - K is excess, and it has three sources: we look at the wrong level, we describe in the wrong frame, or we carry mass, layers kept after their reason has gone. Each has its own remedy: change level, change variable, remove. Two cautions keep the thesis honest. A short rule can be expensive to run, so simplicity of description is not simplicity of computation. And a short rule is a hypothesis, so it must carry its residual, the part it does not explain, as the alarm that says when it is wrong. I collect the evidence from twenty-six earlier posts, give two worked examples, and state five predictions, with what would refute each.

title: It Must Be Simpler Than This
text:
1. Introduction
One evening I opened a physics paper I could not follow, and my first reaction was: it must be simpler than this (A Universe Without a Bottom). I meant it as a feeling. Three weeks later, with twenty-six posts behind me, I think it is a claim, and a testable one.
The posts were about very different things: dashboards, agents, code review, memory in small models, learning rules, time, black holes. Read together, they keep making one move. Something looks complicated; we find that most of the complication came from where we stood, what we measured, or what we refused to throw away; and what remains is short. The dashboard full of numbers becomes the one shape that changed. The agent that reasons from scratch on every run becomes a habit compiled once. Sixteen hours of review a day become a rule that fits in one line.
This paper states that move precisely, says where it comes from, and says where it fails. It is provocative on purpose: it claims that complexity, in most cases that matter to us, is an error of description, and that the right response is to look for a shorter one rather than to build tools for living with the long one.

title: It Must Be Simpler Than This
text:
2. Background
The idea is old, and none of the pieces here are mine.
Description length. Solomonoff and Kolmogorov defined the complexity of an object as the length of the shortest program that produces it (Solomonoff 1964; Kolmogorov 1965). Rissanen turned this into a practical rule for science and statistics, minimum description length: the best model is the one that minimises the length of the model plus the length of the data given the model (Rissanen 1978; Grünwald 2007). Gell-Mann and Lloyd called the first part effective complexity: the length of the regularities, with the randomness set aside (Gell-Mann and Lloyd 1996).
Levels. Simon observed that complex systems that survive are nearly decomposable: hierarchies of parts that interact strongly inside and weakly between, so each level can be described almost on its own (Simon 1962). Anderson warned in the same spirit that each level has its own laws: more is different (Anderson 1972).
Software. Brooks separated essential complexity, which belongs to the problem, from accidental complexity, which belongs to our tools and habits (Brooks 1987); Moseley and Marks argued that most of what makes large systems hard is accidental, mostly state (Moseley and Marks 2006). Gall put the engineering version bluntly: a complex system that works has evolved from a simple system that worked (Gall 1975).
The limits. Wolfram showed that very short rules can produce behaviour with no known shortcut (Wolfram 2002), and Bennett defined logical depth, the time a short program needs to produce its output, to separate the two (Bennett 1988). And on the side of taste, Hossenfelder argued that the wish for simple, beautiful laws has led physics astray as often as it has guided it (Hossenfelder 2018).
What I add is narrower: a bookkeeping of where excess comes from, a rule for practice, and the claim that, in the domains this site covers, the excess is usually large.

title: It Must Be Simpler Than This
text:
3. A minimal definition
Take something we want to describe: a dataset, a codebase, a process, a pattern. Call it x.

A(x), the apparent complexity, is the length of the description we actually use: the raw data we store, the code we keep, the steps we follow.
G is a generator: a rule, model or program that reproduces x up to some error. L(G) is the length of the rule; L(x \mid G) is the length of the residual, what the rule leaves out.
K(x), the intrinsic complexity, is the length of the shortest such pair:


K(x) \;\approx\; \min_G \big[\, L(G) + L(x \mid G) \,\big].
\tag{1}
The excess is what we pay for describing x badly:

E(x) \;=\; A(x) - K(x) \;\geq\; 0 .
\tag{2}
The thesis is that, for most systems people build or study, E is large compared with K. As a bookkeeping device, not a theorem, I split it three ways:

E \;\approx\; E_{\text{level}} + E_{\text{frame}} + E_{\text{mass}} .
\tag{3}
E_{\text{level}} is what we pay for describing parts when the regularity lives in the whole. E_{\text{frame}} is what we pay for describing in a variable where the pattern does not show. E_{\text{mass}} is what we pay for layers whose reason has gone. What is left, K, is the essential part in Brooks’s sense.
Two quantities sit outside this sum and must not be confused with it. The first is depth D(x): the time the shortest generator takes to run (Bennett 1988). A thing can be short and deep. The second is the residual itself, L(x \mid G): it is not waste but the instrument that tells us whether G is still right.
K cannot be computed in general (Kolmogorov 1965). We only ever hold upper bounds: every description we find is one. So the thesis is a claim about how far our current bounds are from the truth, and about where to look to bring them down.

title: It Must Be Simpler Than This
text:
4. The arguments

4.1 Two small worked examples
Short, and it looks it; short, and it does not. Figure 1 stores three patterns of the same size, 128 rows of 255 cells, in three ways: raw, after a general-purpose compressor, and as the shortest Python program I wrote that prints it. Rule 90, a one-line rule, draws nested triangles; the compressor finds most of the regularity (4.0 KB to 375 bytes), and the program needs 134 bytes. Rule 30 is the same one-line rule with a different number. Its output looks random, and the compressor barely helps (1.7 KB), but the program is still 134 bytes. The apparent complexity of Rule 30 is a property of the compressor, not of the pattern.
The third panel is the honest twist. The “coin flips” were drawn from a seeded pseudo-random generator, so they too have a short program, 106 bytes. Looking at the pattern, neither you nor the compressor can tell. This is the uncomputability of K in one picture: we can never be sure there is no shorter rule.



Figure 1. Three patterns of the same size, each stored three ways (log scale). Rule 90 looks simple and is. Rule 30 looks random, yet the same 134-byte program produces it. The “coin flips” came from a seeded generator, so they have a short program too, which nothing in the picture reveals. Computed by figs.py; numbers in results.json.


The simplest complete description is the true one. Figure 2 is the statistical version, the same lesson as in Show What Changed, Not the Data. Forty noisy points come from a quadratic. Fitting polynomials of rising degree, the residual keeps shrinking, so a model judged by fit alone keeps growing. Counting both parts of Equation 1, the total is shortest at degree 2, the law that produced the data. Simplicity here is not a taste; it is the length of a complete description, and it points at the truth.



Figure 2. Two-part description length for polynomial fits to 40 noisy points from a quadratic. The residual (grey) keeps falling as the model grows; the cost of stating the model (amber) keeps rising; their sum (navy) is shortest at degree 2, the true law. A crude MDL count (BIC-style model cost, Gaussian residual), computed by figs.py.




4.2 The three sources, across the site
Table 1 reads the earlier posts against Equation 3. Each row is something that looked complex, and the shorter description the post arrived at.

Table 1. Eleven of the earlier posts, read as reductions of apparent complexity. The last column names the main source of excess in Equation 3.

Figure 3. Three sources of apparent complexity, with examples from the posts in Table 1, and the remedy for each. What remains after all three is the essential part. Schematic, my own.


Level. Temperature is the textbook case: no one describes a gas molecule by molecule. The same move appears whenever the regularity lives in the whole, and Simon’s near-decomposability says why it so often works (Simon 1962). The claim in The Mathematics Still to Come is that machine learning is still looking for this level: its systems are described weight by weight while its behaviour already follows a few smooth laws.
Frame. The same information can be long in one variable and short in another. A dashboard showing levels is long; the same system shown as change is mostly empty. An agent’s history is long; the state it needs to continue is short, and the NVIDIA team found that strong models lose little when the history is replaced by it (Belcak et al. 2026). Code is long; the intent and the checks that define correct code are shorter, which is the thesis of Intent Is the Source.
Mass. The most common source, and the least glamorous. A gate, a ceremony, an adapter or a layer of reasoning was added for a reason; the reason went, the layer stayed. Work Has Mass gives the law: everything you make, you carry. AI makes this source worse, because it lowers the cost of adding a layer, not the cost of carrying it. Here the remedy is not a better description but a shorter system: remove.


4.3 Short is not cheap
Rule 30 has a 134-byte description, but to know its millionth row you must, as far as anyone knows, run it a million times (Wolfram 2002). A short rule can be deep (Bennett 1988). This is where simplicity is most often misread: “it is simple” is heard as “it is easy”.
The posts suggest the answer: pay the depth once. Fast AI uses the large model as a compiler, slow and once, so that what runs every time is short and fast. The Junior Colleague shows the same at the level of single choices: a small model trained on the large model’s own runs took over most decisions in customer-service agents, 86.3% cheaper, as long as it knew when it was unsure. Distillation is the general version (Hinton et al. 2015). The simple thing is not the computation; it is what the computation leaves behind.


4.4 Keep the residual
A short description is a hypothesis. Reality can move in a direction it does not cover, and then the description stays quiet while the world changes, which is the objection a reader raised in What a Quiet Screen Cannot See. The answer there generalises: the residual L(x \mid G) is cheap to watch, and it grows when the rule stops fitting. The rule and its leftover belong together. Throwing away the residual to make the picture cleaner is not simplification; it is blindness.



Figure 4. The rule in practice. Find the generator once, on the slow path; act with it fast; watch what it leaves out; when the leftover grows, go back to the slow path. Schematic, my own.


Put together, the rule is short enough to remember: find the generator, pay its depth once, keep its residual, and remove what neither needs.

title: It Must Be Simpler Than This
text:
5. Predictions and a test protocol
Each prediction names a domain from the site, a measurement, and the result that would refute the thesis there.

P1. Models. Among models trained to the same training loss on the same task, those whose behaviour has a shorter description, measured by prequential coding (Blier and Ollivier 2018), generalise better. Refuted if description length does not predict held-out error once training loss is controlled.
P2. Agents. Replacing an agent’s history with a short written state loses accuracy in proportion to how much of the task’s state cannot be written down. Refuted if the loss is unrelated to that measure, or if long-history agents win consistently on tasks whose state fits on a page.
P3. Processes. Teams that remove a layer whose reason no longer holds (a gate, a ceremony, a handover) deliver faster with no more failures; teams that add layers to AI-assisted work slow down without fewer failures. Refuted if removal raises failure rates in a stepped-wedge trial like the one in Stop Reviewing Pull Requests.
P4. Monitoring. A dashboard that shows only changes of shape plus a residual alarm detects regime shifts at least as early as a full dashboard, for a fraction of the reading time. Refuted if it misses shifts the full dashboard catches, at comparable false-alarm rates.
P5. The global test. Across these domains, when we search seriously for a shorter complete description, we usually find one that does at least as well. Refuted if serious searches mostly come back with descriptions about as long as what we started with: then the world is as complex as it looks, and the essays on this site were lucky.

Protocol. For P1, a benchmark of small models on held-out tasks with prequential description length, as in Blier and Ollivier (2018). For P2, the task suites of Belcak et al. (2026), with tasks annotated for how much of their state is physical or tacit. For P3 and P4, the stepped-wedge design of the review paper: teams adopt the change one at a time in random order, outcomes are measured from logs, not self-reports. P5 is a summary of the other four, judged a year from now.

title: It Must Be Simpler Than This
text:
6. Objections and limitations
“More is different” (Anderson 1972). Higher levels have their own laws that cannot be read off the lower ones. I agree, and it supports the thesis: simplicity is found at the right level, not necessarily at the bottom. Reduction and simplification are different things.
Irreducibility (Wolfram 2002). Some processes have no shortcut. Yes, and Figure 1 shows one. They are short to describe and deep to run; the thesis is about the first, and Section 4.3 deals with the second.
Essential complexity is real (Brooks 1987). Some problems are hard in themselves. The thesis does not say K is small; it says E is usually large compared with K. P5 tests exactly that, and the bench in A Finite State of Mind, with its samples, instruments and living cells, is a place where I expect K to dominate.
The wish for simplicity misleads (Hossenfelder 2018). It can, when simplicity is used as a criterion of truth before the data. Here it is a length to be measured, and every simple description must carry its residual. A beautiful rule with a growing residual is a wrong rule.
Complexity is only moved, never removed. Sometimes. Moving it to the right place, into checks, a compiler or a one-time slow path, is often the point. But the accounting must include where it went: a rule that is short because its complexity was pushed onto users has not reduced E.
Survivorship. The posts in Table 1 are the cases where I found a shorter description; the cases where I did not are not posts. This is the strongest reason to treat Table 1 as illustration, not evidence. The evidence has to come from P1 to P5.
Limits of the formalism. K is uncomputable, so Equation 2 is a bound, not a measurement. The split in Equation 3 is a heuristic: the sources overlap, and the shares cannot be measured separately in general. The worked examples are toys chosen to illustrate, not to prove.

title: It Must Be Simpler Than This
text:
7. Conclusion
Poincaré said the scientist studies nature because it is beautiful, with the beauty of an order the mind can grasp (Poincaré 1914). I would put it in plainer words: we look because we suspect it is shorter than it seems. Most of the time the suspicion is right, because most of the length was ours: the level we chose, the variable we measured, the layers we would not drop. What remains after that is the real thing, short or not, and the residual is how we stay honest about it.
When something looks complex, assume first that the description is wrong. It must be simpler than this, until the residual says it is not.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

title: Never Seen Passing
text:
Essay, November 2026. A philosophical essay about time: why we compress it, what AI adds to that habit, and what we lose when we do. It borrows one image from physics, light, as a metaphor rather than an argument. The two plates are schematics, my own, made with figs.py, and drawn on purpose in a style that is not this site’s usual one: an essay about everything starting to look the same should not look like everything else.
In short. We think of time as something we produce with, so we try to save it, and AI helps us save more. But time is also where we exist: where we think, where we are present to others, where we can be seen. Light offers a strange picture of what happens when time is removed. The fastest thing there is lives no time at all, and no one ever sees it pass: it makes everything else visible and is seen only at the moment it ends. When we compress our days, we drift towards that condition. Our work becomes more visible and we become less so, and the work itself starts to look like everyone else’s. Grasping, inventing and integrating are made of time, and they are where the work becomes ours. AI is a kind of light: fast, everywhere, and, as far as anyone can tell, living nothing on the way. That is fine for a machine, as long as we do not try to become light ourselves.

title: Never Seen Passing
text:
1. Time is where we exist
We speak of time as a resource. We save it, spend it, waste it, invest it. A good day is one in which much was produced; a lost day is one in which little was. In that language, time has value only through what comes out of it, and the obvious goal is to need less of it for the same output. AI fits that language perfectly. It is the best time-saving machine we have built.
But think of the moments when someone had time for you. A teacher who stayed after class. A colleague who did not look at their phone while you explained a problem. A friend who let a silence last. What they gave you was not output. It was presence. For that hour, you existed for them, fully, and they for you.
Having time is not only a way to produce. It is a way to exist. It is the space in which we think rather than react, in which a thought can be followed to its end, in which we can doubt, change our minds, and become someone slightly different from who we were in the morning. Augustine, after long pages of searching for what time is, concluded that it is a kind of stretching of the mind itself, a distentio animi (Augustine of Hippo 1909, XI.26): the mind holding what has been, attending to what is, expecting what will be. Time, on that view, is not something we have. It is something we are stretched across.
And when it shrinks, we shrink with it. The sociologist Hartmut Rosa has described how the technologies that save time leave us feeling shorter of it than ever, because the saved minutes are immediately spent on doing more (Rosa 2013). A meeting becomes a message, a document becomes its summary, a person becomes their deliverables. Little by little, we appear to each other only as outputs: the report arrived, the ticket was closed, the dashboard was updated. The one who produced them is less and less visible.
That is the argument I want to make first. Shortening our time does not only cost us quality. It costs us presence. It makes us harder to see, by others and by ourselves.

title: Never Seen Passing
text:
2. Light is never seen passing
Physics offers an image of this that I cannot forget.
Imagine a photon leaving a star in a distant galaxy. For us, its journey lasts billions of years. Galaxies form and collide while it travels. For the photon, no time passes at all. Einstein’s relativity says that a moving clock runs slow, and the faster it moves, the slower it runs (Einstein 1920). At six tenths of the speed of light, a clock ticks eight times while one at rest ticks ten. At the speed of light, it does not tick at all. Along the path of light, the time lived between departure and arrival, what physicists call proper time, is exactly zero.
A photon has no point of view, and physics allows no frame of reference that moves with light, so this is an image, not an experience. But the image has a second half. We never see light passing. We see by light: everything visible is visible because photons left it and reached us. A photon is seen only at the moment it is absorbed, which is the moment it ends. Light makes everything visible except itself.
That is the picture of where compression leads. The fastest thing in the universe lives nothing on the way and is never seen while it travels. It delivers, perfectly, and disappears into what it delivers.



Figure 1. Four paths between the same two moments, A and B, in the language of special relativity. The path that stays at rest lives ten units of time; at 0.6 c, eight; at 0.9 c, about four; the path of light, none. The slowest path between two moments is the one that holds the most time; the path of light holds none, and is never itself seen. Schematic, my own.

title: Never Seen Passing
text:
3. Time belongs to slow things
Turn the image around, and it says something about us.
We are slow. The Earth carries us around the sun at about thirty kilometres per second, roughly one ten-thousandth of the speed of light. Brian Greene describes everything as moving through spacetime at the same speed: light puts all of it into space, and what is nearly at rest puts nearly all of it into time (Greene 1999, ch. 2). We are almost entirely made of time. It is so present for us, so heavy, because we move so slowly. And as Figure 1 shows, between two moments the slow path is not the wasteful one. It is the one that holds the most time.
Henri Bergson called lived time duration, and gave the simplest example of it I know: “If I want to mix a glass of sugar and water, I must, willy-nilly, wait until the sugar melts” (Bergson 1911, ch. 1). The waiting is not wasted. The melting is the time it takes.
When we compress our days, we are trying, in a small way, to become light: to have the answer without the time between the question and the answer. And light is precisely the thing for which nothing happens on the way.

title: Never Seen Passing
text:
4. Fast, and the same
AI enters with a clear message: you can do more in less time. I agree, and I have argued for it in Fast AI. Much of our work is repetitive, and doing it faster is simply good. Not all of our hours are worth living slowly, and I am glad to give some of them away.
But the message carries an unspoken second half: since it was done fast, it is done. Speed tells us how long something took. It tells us nothing about whether it was worth doing, or whether it is any good.
And there is a second effect, which I have started to see in my own work. When a process takes weeks, we live inside it, making small choices all along the way: what to show first, what to leave out, which word fits. The result carries the marks of the path, and through them, of the person who walked it. When it takes minutes, we barely see the process. We judge the result by whether it looks right, and “looks right” has a centre of gravity: the plausible, which is close to what has been done before. I see it when people use Claude, or any assistant, to build dashboards and reports. Each one is better than what most of us would have made by hand in the same time. Together, they look alike: the same cards, the same row of key figures, the same soft palette. The same look and feel, everywhere.
Research points the same way. In an experiment by Doshi and Hauser, stories written with ideas from a language model were judged more creative on average, but were also more similar to one another (Doshi and Hauser 2024). Each person gained. The collection lost variety. One experiment is not a law, and every era has had its templates. But the mechanism is easy to see: light between two points always takes the same path. Only the slow traveller can wander, and arrive somewhere no one else has been.



Figure 2. Above, paths made slowly wander, cross and end in different places, each with its own mark. Below, paths made fast go straight, and all arrive at the same plausible result. Schematic, my own.


This is where the two halves of the argument meet. Sameness is what invisibility looks like from the outside. When the path disappears, so do the marks of the one who walked it. The result is good, and it is everyone’s, and so it is no one’s.

title: Never Seen Passing
text:
5. Where the work becomes ours
Three kinds of time behave like Bergson’s sugar, and each is a place where the work becomes ours.
The time to grasp. I can read an explanation in two minutes and understand it a week later. A summary shortens the reading, not the grasping, because the grasping happens in me. No one can understand something on my behalf, and what I have understood, I can explain in my own words.
The time to invent. Poincaré described weeks of failure on a mathematical problem, then finding the answer the moment he stepped onto a bus, thinking of something else (Poincaré 1914, bk. I, ch. 3). Graham Wallas later named the stages: preparation, incubation, illumination, verification (Wallas 1926). AI helps with the first and the last. Incubation, the middle, looks exactly like doing nothing, which is why it is the first thing we cut. It is also where an idea takes the shape of the mind that holds it.
The time to integrate. You can roll out a tool in a day. You cannot roll out a new practice in a day, because a practice is what people do once they have stopped thinking about the tool, and it becomes a team’s own only by being lived.
These are not slow because we are inefficient. They are made of time, the way a melody is: play it ten times faster and you do not get the same melody sooner, you get noise. And they are where we become visible in what we make. An idea we received carries no trace of us. An idea we grasped, invented or integrated carries our mark.

title: Never Seen Passing
section: 6. The objection: are we not more visible than ever?
text:
6. The objection: are we not more visible than ever?
The strongest objection to this essay is simple. Those who produce more and faster are surely more visible, not less. Their reports are everywhere, their names in every feed, their dashboards on every screen. In a world that sees through output, speed looks like the best way to be seen.
I think this confuses two kinds of visibility, and light shows the difference. When you look at a lit room, you see the table, the books, the faces. You do not see the light. Speed makes the work visible. It does not make the person visible; it can make them vanish into the work, the way light vanishes into what it illuminates. A colleague who ships ten reports a week is very visible as a source of reports. Whether anyone knows how they think, what they doubt, what they would have done differently, is another matter. That second visibility takes time: time to say something that is not yet a deliverable, and time for someone else to listen.
There is a softer objection too. Every generation has said new tools would make people shallow, and each time people found new ways to think deeply with them. Perhaps AI, by taking the tedious parts, gives us more time to exist. I think this is half right. But freed time does not stay free by itself. In 1930, Keynes imagined that productivity would bring his grandchildren a fifteen-hour week (Keynes 1931). The productivity came; we spent it on more output. The time to think has no defender. It does not appear on a dashboard, and it looks like idleness. Unless someone protects it on purpose, it is the first thing the saved hours will be spent on.

title: Never Seen Passing
text:
7. Let the machines be light
There is a way to read the metaphor that is not a warning.
AI is a kind of light. It is fast, it is everywhere, and, as far as anyone can tell, it lives nothing on the way. It makes things visible: patterns in data, options in a design, the shape of a problem. It does not need to be seen itself, and it is not diminished by having no time. That is fine. That is what light is for.
The mistake would be to compete with it at its own speed: to try to become light ourselves, delivering everywhere and living nothing. We will lose that race, and we will disappear in the effort. The better division of labour is the one the universe already has: light travels, and slow things stay where they can be seen.
So when AI saves a day, I try to ask where the day went, not only what else can be shipped. I try to keep the parts of the process that make the work mine: the question, the structure, what to leave out. And I try to keep some time empty. The Greek word for leisure, scholē, is the root of our word school; Josef Pieper called leisure the basis of culture, a time in which we can receive what we cannot produce (Pieper 1952).
Light, after all, shows only what is there. Point it at an empty room and it shows an empty room; ask it for a dashboard and bring nothing of your own, and it shows the plausible, the same dashboard everyone else received. That is the sameness we saw earlier, seen from the other side. The light is not the problem. What matters is what we put in front of it: a question we have lived with, a doubt, a way of seeing that took time to form. That is the part only slow things can bring.
A photon crosses the whole universe and lives nothing. It lights up everything, and no one ever sees it pass.
We are slow. That is why we have time, and why we can be seen.
Let the machines be light. We are what it falls on.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
text:
Fast and Local AI · Part 4 of 4 · Read the whole series
In short. For the whole history of deep learning, the weights of a network have been written by an optimizer. Since 2023, a growing body of work has trained special models to read weights or to generate them. The new post claims something different: a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, can read a network’s raw weights and say what it was trained to do, and can write weights directly, around a goal stated in plain language. It names the game a policy was trained on, finds the induction heads of a small transformer without running it, fixes a stuck control policy in one reply, writes game players from scratch that beat PPO trained for 100 million steps, and edits 0.016% of a 0.8-billion-parameter model to stop it looping, which raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%. My reading: the results are real, but narrower than the headline. The model is best at turning a program it understands into neural form, and at removing an obstacle it can find; the authors’ own control shows it could not add an ability a model lacked. That shape suits Fast AI very well. Fast AI already uses the large model once, before the loop, as a compiler; weight-space programming lets it compile into the small network itself, repair that network without a GPU cluster, and ship the fix as a patch of a few hundred kilobytes. On premise, the hard question is what leaves the building: a specification can, private data should not, and trained weights carry some of that data. I sketch an incubator that respects this line, and the experiment that would show whether it is worth building.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
text:
Weights were for optimizers
A neural network is, in the end, a long list of numbers. A program written in Python can be read by a person; a list of 17,253 floating-point numbers cannot, at least not by anyone I know. So the division of labour has been stable for decades. People write the architecture, the data and the loss. An optimizer, usually a variant of gradient descent, writes the weights. People then study the result from the outside, by running it.
The post’s authors put this well. We have used large language models for a few years to optimize text: prompts and the programs around them (Khattab et al. 2024; Agrawal et al. 2026), whole harnesses (Lee et al. 2026), and the training code that trains models (Karpathy 2026). The justification was that text has no gradient, and a person can improve code by hand, so a language model could too. Weights were the exception. “Humans can ‘optimize’ code by hand,” they write, “but they can’t ‘optimize’ neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms” (Takehi et al. 2026).
The claim of the post is that this exception is ending. If it holds, it changes something I care about more than the benchmark scores: how a large model can help a small one.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
section: What came before: four ways to touch a weight, 2023 to 2026
text:
What came before: four ways to touch a weight, 2023 to 2026
To see what is new, it helps to sort the earlier work by two questions: does it read weights or write them, and is the reader or writer a tool built for the job, a model trained for the job, or a general model used as it is? Figure 1 places the main lines of work.



Figure 1. Work from 2023 to 2026 that reads or writes neural network weights, sorted by who does the reading or writing. The placement is my own reading of the cited work; the right-hand column was empty until this year. Schematic, my own.


Reading, with tools built for the job. Mechanistic interpretability traces circuits (Olah et al. 2020) and found the induction heads that let a transformer copy earlier text, with a method that multiplies weight matrices without running the model (Elhage et al. 2021). Sparse autoencoders split activations into nameable features (Bricken et al. 2023; Cunningham et al. 2023), and circuit tracing draws whole computational graphs (Ameisen et al. 2025).
Reading, with models trained for the job. Weight-space networks are trained to take another network’s weights as input and predict its properties, such as accuracy or the data it was trained on (Navon et al. 2023; Zhou et al. 2023; Lim et al. 2024). Language models joined in, as explainers of single neurons (Bills et al. 2023), as readers of fine-tuning differences (Goel et al. 2025) and activations (Karvonen et al. 2025; Fraser-Taliente et al. 2026), and, this autumn, of weights directly (Kabra et al. 2026).
Writing, with tools. Task arithmetic adds and subtracts the weight differences of fine-tuned models (Ilharco et al. 2023); TIES, DARE and evolutionary search made merging more robust (Yadav et al. 2023; Yu et al. 2024; Akiba et al. 2025). Refusal in many chat models is carried by one direction, and removing it from the weights removes the behaviour (Arditi et al. 2024); facts can be located and edited (Meng et al. 2022). Tracr compiled small programs directly into transformer weights (Lindner et al. 2023), and gradient-free optimizers write weights by trial and error (Salimans et al. 2017; Malladi et al. 2023; Qiu et al. 2026).
Writing, with models trained for the job. Generative models produce checkpoints (Peebles et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2024); hypernetworks turn a task description or a few prompts into adapters (Phang et al. 2023; Charakorn et al. 2025; Liang et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025). SEAL lets a model write its own fine-tuning data, but gradients still apply the update (Zweiger et al. 2025).
The pattern across these four boxes is the one the post points out: “either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing” (Takehi et al. 2026). The one exception they cite, AdderBoard, has coding agents set the weights of a tiny transformer by hand (Papailiopoulos 2026). The right-hand column of Figure 1 is what the post claims to fill.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
text:
What the post claims
The authors define the idea in one sentence: “In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all” (Takehi et al. 2026).
Stated a little more formally, the claim has three parts. Let W be the weights of a network with a known architecture, and let M be a general-purpose language model.

Read. Given W as text or as tensors, and a question q about the network’s behaviour, M answers q correctly more often than chance, without running the network.
Fix. Given W, a goal g and little or no feedback, M produces W' = W + \Delta with a small \Delta, such that W' meets g better than W.
Write. Given only the architecture and a description of the task, M produces W from zero that performs well, with no data, no loss and no gradient.

The interesting resource is not tokens but forward passes: how often M is allowed to run the network to see what it does. Several experiments allow none.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
text:
The eight experiments
Table 1 gathers the setup and the main result of each experiment, as reported.

Table 1. The eight experiments of Takehi and colleagues (Takehi et al. 2026), in their order. The games in Experiment 1 are the authors’ grid versions; MinAtar (Young and Tian 2019) and Kinetix (Matthews et al. 2025) are standard benchmarks.

2

3

4

5

6

8

The zero-shot players of Experiment 5 deserve their own table, because they are the cleanest test of writing: no data, no tools, no rollouts, one reply.

Table 2. Mean score over 1,000 episodes in three MinAtar games, from the post. PPO is the best of 3 to 10 seeds.

How the model does it matters more than the scores. In every case where the post shows the reasoning, the model does not search the weight space. It understands the network as a program. In Breakout, “Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position.” In Go, it writes 336 lines of Python that mark stones and liberties in the first layers, propagate along chains in the middle ones, and score captures and saves in the last. In the car, it adds “a small separate path through a few units per layer” that backs the car up and then switches off. When reading, it rediscovers, unprompted, the weight-multiplication method that Elhage and colleagues used to find induction heads (Elhage et al. 2021).
Experiment 8 is the headline and the most instructive. Figure 2 plots its table.



Figure 2. Experiment 8: Qwen3.5-0.8B after Astra’s weight edit, for three budgets of forward passes. The last panel is the share of MATH-500 answers that run to the 32,768-token limit, which falls only with the largest budget. Data from Takehi and colleagues (Takehi et al. 2026), their table; chart my own.


The base model loops: it repeats itself and rarely finishes (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the token limit; Qwen’s own model card warns of this). Astra traced the loops to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19 and subtracted it from 64 output columns in each, 131,072 weights in all. This is, as the authors note, close in spirit to removing refusal by deleting one direction (Arditi et al. 2024), and to recent work on why reasoning models loop (Pipis et al. 2025). Because looping is not specific to mathematics, instruction following improved too.
Then comes the control I respect most in the post. The authors tried the same thing on Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops. Nothing worked: MATH-500 went from 6.8% to at most 7.7%, a gain Astra itself called not established. Their conclusion is careful: “Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked.”

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
text:
My reading
What I keep. Three things seem solid to me, even at this early stage.
First, reading without running works on small networks, at least for coarse questions. Experiment 3 is the convincing one: with the input and output layers removed, nothing in the weights says which dimension is which letter, and still the model finds the copying heads that a measurement confirms, with no false positives. That is not pattern-matching on the first layer. It is structural reasoning about matrices.
Second, writing works where a program exists. Breakout has a clean algorithm (go where the ball will land), and the written network scores 20 times PPO at 500 million steps. Seaquest has no such short program (oxygen, divers, enemies, timing) and the written network reaches 60% of PPO. That gradient is the most informative thing in Table 2. It says weight-space programming is, at heart, compilation by understanding: Tracr did it for programs written in RASP (Lindner et al. 2023); here the program lives in the model’s reasoning and the target is an ordinary MLP.
Third, a small, stated edit can fix a large failure. A 0.016% change that is explained in a sentence (“this direction causes the loops; remove it”) is a very different object from a full fine-tune. It can be reviewed.
What I let go of. The framing that the model “made Qwen better at math” overstates the result, and the authors’ own Gemma control says so. The edit let the model finish answers it could already work out. That is valuable, but it is repair, not teaching.
I would also read the PPO comparisons with care. PPO on a 32-unit MLP is probably a weak baseline; 517 against 25 says as much about how hard a small network is to train with reinforcement learning as about the written one. The comparison the post does not run is a written network used as the starting point for PPO.
Forward passes are feedback too. In Experiment 8, ten or twenty-five passes barely moved the loops (87% and 86% still hit the limit), IFEval was lower at 25 than at 10, and then fifty passes changed everything. With one edit per budget, a scaling curve and a lucky search look the same.
And the samples are small: four games, three shapes, three languages, three sycophant pairs, one large model. Experiment 7 failed from weights alone. The model is one that most readers, including me, cannot try. None of this makes the results wrong; it makes them sparks, which is what the title says.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
section: A more advanced mind shaping a smaller one
text:
A more advanced mind shaping a smaller one
Here is the part that interests me most, and it is not in the post.
There have been, until now, two ways for a large model to make a small one better. The first is distillation: the large model produces outputs, and the small one learns to imitate them by gradient descent (Hinton et al. 2015). Many small models of the last two years were made this way, sometimes combined with pruning (Muralidharan et al. 2024). The second is a trained generator: a hypernetwork that maps a description to weights (Charakorn et al. 2025; Liang et al. 2025). In both, the small model’s weights are still written by an optimizer, from examples.
Weight-space programming adds a third way, and it is strange. The large model does not show the small one examples. It reads the small one’s weights, forms a theory of what it computes, and changes it. Table 3 puts the three side by side.

Table 3. Three ways a large model can shape a small one. The first two columns summarize the cited work; the third summarizes the post, and the last two rows are my reading.









Distillation
Trained generator
Weight-space programming




What the teacher gives
Examples of its behaviour
A learned map from task to weights
A diagnosis and an edit


Who writes the weights
The student’s optimizer

The teacher, directly


Needs data
Much
Many trained checkpoints
Little or none


Explains itself
No
No
In plain language


Good at
Transferring broad ability
Fast adaptation within a family
Starting points, repairs, audits


Weak at
Removing a specific flaw

Adding an ability the student lacks



The human analogy is tempting, and it is half right. A good teacher does not only give examples; they notice the specific misconception behind a run of mistakes and address that one thing. Experiment 8 is exactly that: one misconception (a direction that never lets go), one correction. But a human teacher works through the student’s own learning. Here the teacher bypasses it and edits the mind itself. That is more powerful, and less safe: the student has no say, and nothing in the student’s own experience confirms the change. It is the difference between a tutor and a surgeon. We accept surgery, but we ask surgeons to state what they will cut and why, to check afterwards, and to keep records.
The Gemma result also fits the analogy uncomfortably well. You can clear an obstacle in a mind; you cannot, by editing, give it understanding it never formed. Ability still comes from learning. What a more advanced mind can do is give a smaller one a better start, remove what blocks it, and check it before it goes out into the world.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
text:
An incubator for small networks
That suggests a concrete design, which I will call an incubator. It is a loop around ordinary training, in which a large model plays the role of a mentor to a small network (Figure 3).



Figure 3. An incubator for small networks. The large model writes a starting point, ordinary training grows it, the large model examines and repairs it, and the loop repeats while each edit pays for itself; release comes with an audit note and the weight diff. The labels above the cards say where each stage can run on premise: at most the specification leaves, and it can be confidential too. Schematic, my own; it shows a proposal, not a result.



Conceive. From a specification in plain language, the mentor writes a first network of the target size, as a program in neural form, the way Astra wrote the Breakout and Go players. Where the task has a known algorithm, this start may already be good; where it does not, it is at least structured.
Grow. Ordinary training, on real data, from that start. This is where ability comes from, and where the Gemma lesson applies: the mentor cannot skip it.
Examine. The mentor reads the trained weights, with a small budget of probes, looking for known failure modes: loops, shortcuts, a direction that tracks the user’s opinion (the sycophancy of Experiment 7), dead units, a policy stuck in a local minimum (Experiment 4).
Operate. A small edit, stated in a sentence, kept only if held-out tests agree. Then back to training, so that the network can absorb the change.
Release. The network goes out with an audit note: what was examined, what was found, what was changed, and the weight diff itself.

The economics are simple to state. Let C_\text{train}(s) be the cost of training from a starting point s to a target quality, C_\text{write} the mentor’s cost to write the start, and C_\text{fix} the cost of each examine-and-operate round. The incubator is worth it when

\begin{aligned}
&C_\text{write} + C_\text{train}(s_\text{written}) + k \, C_\text{fix}\\
&\quad < \; C_\text{train}(s_\text{random}),
\end{aligned}

or, more often in practice, when it reaches a quality that plain training does not reach at all, as with the stuck car. The post gives hints on both sides: a written start can be very good (Table 2), and a single repair can be worth more than any amount of extra training (the car never succeeded in 256 episodes after a billion steps). It gives no measurement of the left-hand side. That is the first experiment anyone should run.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
section: What it means for Fast AI on premise
text:
What it means for Fast AI on premise
On this site I have argued for what I call Fast AI: experts learn slowly, once, and then act fast on habit, so the large model should be used before the loop, as a compiler, and fast, explainable models should run the process (see Fast AI). I have also argued that local AI will be an ecosystem of small specialists, a shared memory and a thin harness, not one large model made small (see An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle). Many of the places where this matters most run on premise: a factory, a hospital, a bank, an administration, where hardware is modest, latency is tight, and data may not leave the building. Weight-space programming touches that picture in five places.

1. Compile into the weights, not only into the memory
In Fast AI, the large model compiles a task into a structured memory (a knowledge graph experts can inspect) and small models run on it. Weight-space programming adds a second compilation target: the small network itself. Experiment 5 is exactly this, with the rules and source code of a game turned into a 600→32→32→6 network in one reply. The resulting network is tiny, runs in microseconds on a CPU or an NPU, and needs no large model at run time. That is the Fast AI cost profile: slow and expensive once, cheap every time after.
I would keep one rule from the Fast AI essay: let deep learning perceive and trees decide. If a business rule is known and stable, a decision tree is cheaper, faster and easier to audit than any network, written or trained. A written network earns its place where the decision sits on top of perception (the rule needs features a tree cannot see), or where it must run fused with a perception model on the same accelerator. Writing a network to imitate a rule you already have in a table is a step backwards.


2. The mentor visits; it does not stay
The large model’s cost is paid at build time and at repair time, never per decision. In Experiment 8 the whole repair took fifty forward passes of the 0.8B model and one session of the large one; the post does not report the large model’s own cost. Compare that with the agent that “reads the manual every morning”, which pays the large model on every run. For an on-premise customer, this is the difference between a recurring dependence on a remote model and an occasional visit by a specialist. Table 4 summarizes where each part would run.

Table 4. Where each part of an incubated small model would run in an on-premise deployment. My own proposal, based on the setups of Experiments 5, 6 and 8 (Takehi et al. 2026).







Stage
Where it can run
What it needs to see




Write a first network (large model)
Anywhere, including remote
The specification and the architecture


Train it (ordinary optimizer)
On premise
Private data


Examine it (large model, a few forward passes)
On premise, or remote if weights may leave
The trained weights and some probes


Repair it (large model, a Python kernel)
Same as above
The weights; no gradients


Run it (the small network only)
On premise, CPU or NPU
Live inputs





3. Repair without a GPU cluster
On-premise teams rarely have the infrastructure, or the data pipeline, to fine-tune again every time a model misbehaves. The Qwen repair used a Python kernel “over the weights (no GPU)” and no training at all. The forward passes are not free, though: fifty of them, at an average of 64 answers that mostly ran to 32,768 tokens, come to the order of a hundred million generated tokens (my rough estimate from the post’s settings). For a 0.8-billion-parameter model that is hours on one GPU, not a job for a CPU, but it is one machine, not a cluster. The edit changed 131,072 weights: about half a megabyte in 32-bit floats, a quarter in 16-bit (my arithmetic). That is a patch, in the software sense. It can be signed, shipped, applied and rolled back like any other patch, and a customer can keep the base model they already validated.
The limit is the one the Gemma control drew. A patch can remove a failure that hides an ability (loops, a stuck policy, a direction that tracks the user’s opinion). It will not add an ability the model lacks; that still needs training, and data.


4. What leaves the building
This is the part I would think hardest about before selling anything. Private data should not leave the building. A specification usually can, but not always: in Experiment 5 the mentor also read the game’s source code, and on premise the equivalent (business rules, process logic) can be confidential too. Trained weights sit in between: they are shaped by their training data, and published attacks have extracted verbatim training examples from language models (Carlini et al. 2021). Sending a model trained on patient records to a remote mentor for “examination” is therefore a data transfer, whatever the contract calls it.
The setups in the post suggest a clean split. Writing from a specification (Experiments 5 and 6) needs no data at all, so it can be done by any mentor the customer is willing to show the specification to. Training happens on premise, on private data. Examining and repairing need the trained weights, so either the weights may leave, or the mentor must run inside. Today, only a frontier model has shown this ability at this level, and only in one lab’s hands. Whether an open model that a customer can run locally can do the examination is, to me, the most important open question for on-premise use. Until it is answered, the safe on-premise recipe is: write remotely, train and run locally, and examine locally with the tools we already have.


5. Audit before deployment, and review the intent
Regulated customers ask what a model does before they let it run. Reading weights could add a new kind of evidence: not only “it passed these tests” but “here is what it computes, here is what we looked for and did not find”. Experiment 7 is a warning, though: from weights alone, Astra saw many differences between an honest and a sycophantic model and could not say which mattered. Reading should add to evaluation, not replace it.
And every edit needs a stated intent. A 131,072-weight diff is not something a person will read; “remove the direction that causes loops in layers 15 and 19” is. That is the shift I argued for code in Review the Intent, Not the Diff: humans own the intent, machines own the implementation, tests check one against the other. On premise, the intent note, the diff and the test results should ship together, and the customer should be able to refuse the patch.
A decision model of the kind I analysed in The Junior Colleague is the natural first candidate for all five: small, narrow, often close to a program, trained on the agent’s own states, and running next to the agent on the customer’s machine.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
text:
Where it breaks

Scale. The networks that fit in context have at most 171,664 weights. The 0.8B edit used a Python kernel and fifty forward passes, and changed one direction. Nothing yet shows that a model can understand a large network as a whole, rather than find one handle in it.
Tasks without a program. Writing works best where a short algorithm exists. Many tasks we give small models (perception, language, judgement) have none, and there the mentor can only repair and audit.
Written starts that resist training. Nothing in the post tests a written network as a starting point for gradient training. Weights set by reasoning can push tanh units into saturation, where gradients vanish, so the Grow stage may stall or simply erase the written structure.
Adversarial weights. A reader that can be fooled by weights crafted to look benign is an attack surface. None of the experiments tests this.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
text:
What I am not claiming
Not that gradient descent is on its way out: the best results in the post still come from networks trained first or from tasks simple enough to program. Not that the incubator works; it is a design, with its test below. Not that written networks should replace decision trees where the rules are known. Nothing about GPT-6 Astra beyond what the post reports. And not that a model reading weights understands them the way we hope; it may have found a heuristic for small MLPs that fails silently at scale.

title: The Teacher Who Writes the Weights
text:
What would prove me wrong

A model that adds an ability by editing. If a weight edit, with no training, gives a model a skill it measurably lacked (not one hidden by a failure like looping), my distinction between repair and teaching falls. A replication of the Gemma control with a positive result would be the place to look.
Written starts that do not help training. If PPO or supervised training from a mentor-written start reaches the same quality, at the same total cost, as training from a random start, the “Conceive” stage of the incubator is useless.
Repairs that do not survive training. If a stated edit, followed by more training, is reliably undone, edits are cosmetic and the incubator’s loop does not converge.
No local mentor. If, by the end of 2027, no open model that runs on a single server can repeat Experiment 3 or the Qwen repair, then weight-space programming stays a remote service, and its on-premise value is limited to writing from specifications.
Gradient-free optimizers that match it. If evolution strategies or forward-pass fine-tuning (Qiu et al. 2026; Malladi et al. 2023), given the same fifty forward passes, find an edit as good as Astra’s on Qwen, then the reasoning is not what made the difference, and a cheap local optimizer would do.

The experiment I would run first is small: three MinAtar games, a 32-unit MLP, and four arms at equal compute: PPO from zero, PPO from a written start, the written network alone, and PPO with one examine-and-operate round halfway. I would run it twice, to keep two questions apart. First with the strongest mentor available, to test the incubator itself; then with an open model on one on-premise server, to test whether a local mentor is enough. If the second and fourth arms win the first run, the incubator is worth building; the second run says whether it can be built inside the building. If not, I will have learned something too.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.
Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.

The views in this analysis are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.
