title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text: Evenings with Physics · Part 3 of 4 · Read the whole series

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
section: Two ideas that would not stay apart
text:
Two ideas that would not stay apart
In A Universe Without a Bottom I left two thoughts side by side. The first: maybe nothing creates everything. The second: maybe there are grains inside grains, with no final layer.
I treated them as separate questions. A few days later they started to look like one question. And the black hole formula, which I thought said there must be a floor, turned out to say something stranger.
I am still not a physicist. This is still curiosity. But I think I asked the earlier questions slightly wrong.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Nothing is not empty
In the last essay I called infinite temperature “the closest thing to nothing.” Every possibility equally likely. No preference, no structure.
That was half wrong. A state where every possibility is equally likely is not a state with zero information. It is the state with the most possibilities: maximum entropy. You cannot tell the possibilities apart, but they are all there.
This matters because of where the model points. For several years Susskind has argued that this exact system, at infinite temperature, describes de Sitter space: a universe with nothing in it except a horizon around the observer. An empty universe like this carries the largest entropy any region can have. Its horizon is covered with tiles, just like a black hole.
So the two images in my first essay may be the same image. “Nothing” and “a surface that knows everything” could be one thing, seen from different sides.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
A universe with one state
Then I found a result that seemed to say the opposite.
Some universes are closed: travel in a straight line long enough and you come back to where you started. Our universe might be one of them. Over the last few years several groups calculated how many different states such a universe can be in, using the newest tools of quantum gravity. The answer kept coming out the same: one.
One state. Not a large number, not a small number. One. The whole universe, stars and galaxies included, would carry less information than a single coin toss. There is nothing to choose between, so there is nothing to know.
The physicists themselves did not like this. Our universe clearly has more than one possibility in it. I am writing this sentence and not another one. So what went wrong?

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Someone has to be inside
The answer proposed by Harlow, Usatyuk and Zhao is simple to say. The calculation forgot the observer.
It described the universe as if from outside. But a closed universe has no outside. Nobody can stand there and look at it. The philosopher Thomas Nagel called the dream of perfectly objective knowledge the view from nowhere: the world seen from no particular place. Here the view from nowhere is not just hard to reach. It returns nothing.
So put an observer inside, treat the edge of that observer as a kind of boundary, and the many possibilities come back.
One warning, because the word is dangerous. “Observer” here does not mean a mind, a consciousness or a person. In these calculations an observer is any physical system with a limited number of internal states that can keep a record. A clock would do. A detector would do. Nothing mystical is happening. What changes is that there is now a reference point.
There is a catch, and I find it beautiful. How much of the universe the observer can describe depends on how much the observer can hold. A bigger observer, with more internal states, sees a richer and more accurate universe. A tiny one sees a blurry one.



Figure 1. How much the observer can hold. The same toy universe, described by observers that can keep more and more record. Each keeps only the largest-scale patterns it can afford; the tiny one sees a blur, the large one sees the filaments. The last panel is the whole toy universe, a view nobody inside actually has. Below: how faithful each description is, against the size of the observer. A toy, not a physics simulation; the code is in figs.py.


So the information in the universe is not simply “out there.” It exists between the universe and something inside it. This is close to an idea Carlo Rovelli proposed in 1996, relational quantum mechanics: physical properties are not owned by things, they exist only relative to other things. The new calculations do not prove this view. But they point the same way.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Two kinds of nothing
Now put the two results next to each other.

No observer: one state. Zero alternatives. Nothing to know.
One observer at the centre: a horizon full of tiles. Every alternative equally likely. Everything possible, nothing distinguishable.

Both look featureless. Both feel like “nothing.” But they are featureless for opposite reasons. The first has no possibilities. The second has all of them, and no way to tell them apart.



Figure 2. Two kinds of nothing. Left: a closed universe seen from nowhere, stars and galaxies included, counts as one state; all the probability sits on it. Right: put one observer at the centre and a horizon appears, covered with tiles; every pattern of tiles is equally likely, so every bar has the same height. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


Here is my step. Maybe these are not two different universes. Maybe they are the same universe, once without a reference point and once with one. Without one, the universe is nothing. With one, it is everything its horizon can hold.
This is less of a leap than I first thought. De Sitter space, taken as a whole, is itself a closed universe, so the one-state result should apply to it too. And in 2022, Chandrasekaran, Longo, Penington and Witten showed that the entropy of a de Sitter horizon only becomes well defined once an observer is included, and that empty de Sitter space is then the state of maximum entropy. As far as I know, nobody has put these results together in exactly this way. But the pieces fit.
Philosophers got here long before the equations. Hegel opened his Science of Logic (1812) with this very puzzle: pure being, with no determination at all, cannot be told apart from pure nothing. What sets things in motion, for Hegel, is becoming, the passage between the two. Two centuries later, physics seems to add one thing. What turns nothing into everything is a point of view.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Grains again
In the first essay I was stuck on a contradiction. History suggests the layers never end. The black hole formula says a region can hold only a limited amount of information, so it cannot hide infinite layers. There must be a floor.
Remember the 1987 bubble: a tiny pocket of dense energy that grows into a new universe. From outside it looks like a small black hole that disappears. From inside it is a whole cosmos.
Physicists have known for a long time that this is uncomfortable. A small black hole should hold only a little information. How can a whole universe fit inside? Wheeler called this kind of object a “bag of gold.”
The one-state result changes the question. At first, seen from outside, the bubble is a small black hole, and that black hole does carry some information on its surface. But the bubble then pinches off and becomes a separate closed universe. From that moment, with nothing of ours inside it, it counts as one state. It costs us almost nothing. From the inside, with its own observers, it is everything.



Figure 3. A bag of gold. Left: a slice of space drawn as a surface. Our universe sits above, falling into a small black hole; through the narrow neck (red), the horizon, it opens onto a large closed universe below. Right: the neck closes and the bubble pinches off. Counted from outside, it then carries one state. From inside, nothing has changed. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


And the same flip can repeat:

Inside that grain, a new bubble forms. To the grain, it counts as one state. To its own inhabitants, it is a cosmos.
Our universe might be a grain in someone else’s. To them, we would be one state. To us, we are everything.




Figure 4. Grains inside grains. Each panel zooms into one grain of the panel before it (circled in red). Seen from the grain around it, each one counts as a single state; seen by its own inhabitants, it is a whole universe, with grains of its own. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


Leibniz imagined something like this three centuries ago. In his Monadology (1714) he wrote that each portion of matter is like a garden full of plants, and that each branch of every plant is again such a garden. He also said that his ultimate units, the monads, “have no windows”: nothing comes in, nothing goes out. A grain that counts as one state from outside is a monad without windows.
Pascal, whose fear of infinite spaces I quoted last time, wrote in the same Pensées that we stand between two infinities, the infinitely large and the infinitely small, unable to see either end. He took this as a limit of human sight. Perhaps it is more than that. Perhaps each end is hidden by construction, from wherever anyone stands.
The contradiction disappears. Each level has a floor, but only for whoever counts from outside. The chain can go on forever because each grain is almost invisible to the one around it. The black hole formula does not forbid infinite layers. It only forbids seeing them.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
Where information begins
I ended the first essay with “from nothing to nothing,” and the hope that the middle still matters. I would now say it differently.
Not from nothing to nothing. Nothing from outside, everything from inside, at every level, with no last level.
That makes my earlier ending more literal. If a universe has only one state until something inside it can keep a record, then the middle is not just where meaning lives. It is where information starts to exist. Not because anyone is conscious, but because something is somewhere.
This brings the question back to the usual subject of this blog. A large language model has a strangely similar shape. Before you ask it anything, it holds an enormous space of possible answers, all weighted, none chosen. Seen from outside, it is a horizon of possibilities with nothing in particular in it. An answer appears only when a question arrives from a particular place. Asking is not reading out something already written down. It is the moment the possibilities narrow into one.



Figure 5. An analogy, not physics. Left: a space of possible answers, drawn flat, before anyone asks: everything weighted, nothing chosen. Right: a question arrives from a particular place, and the possibilities narrow. The “spread” is the entropy of each picture, in bits. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


This is an analogy, not physics. I already took the first essay’s question to an image generator in Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary. But the lesson may be the same at both scales. Information is not stored somewhere, waiting. It happens at the boundary between a system and whatever stands inside it, or in front of it.
I started by believing the universe must be simple. Maybe it is. From outside, it is as simple as anything can be: one state. The complexity is a view from inside. And we are inside.

title: Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside
text:
What I am not claiming

The one-state result comes mostly from simplified models, often with gravity in two dimensions. Physicists find it fairly convincing, but it is not settled for our universe.
Linking it to the de Sitter results is my own reading. As far as I know, none of the papers below states it this way.
Whether a 1987-style bubble really becomes a closed universe in the sense of these calculations is an open question.
The idea that the nesting never ends is speculation, not a result.
Hegel, Leibniz, Pascal and the comparison with AI are echoes, not evidence. They show the idea is old, not that it is true.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
Agentic Coding · Part 3 of 5 · Read the whole series
Abstract. Each generation of programming has turned what people used to write into something the machine generates: machine code into the output of assemblers, assembly into the output of compilers, boilerplate into the output of frameworks. I argue that agentic coding, in which a language model plans, edits, runs and repairs code inside a loop, is the next step on this ladder, and a larger one than it looks. The thesis is that the agentic loop is both the next IDE and the next programming language. I define a program as a tuple P = (I, T, K, \Gamma) of intent, executable checks, context and tools, and the agent as a stochastic compiler that is correct only up to the checks. From this definition follow four arguments (historical, structural, economic, empirical), one central consequence (the precision of the new language is the strength of its checks), and four predictions that can be measured within a few years. I end with the strongest objections, including Dijkstra’s, and the evidence that currently cuts against me.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
1. Introduction
Programming languages are usually described by their syntax and semantics. A more useful description, for the argument here, is what a person has to write and what the machine produces from it. By that measure, the history of programming is a ladder. On each rung, people stopped writing one thing and started writing something more abstract, while the old thing kept existing as output.



Figure 1. Schematic. Each generation of programming turned what people used to write into what the step above generates. The examples are illustrative.


Since code-generating language models appeared (Chen et al. 2021), the obvious question has been whether they are a better autocomplete or something else. Andrej Karpathy framed neural networks as “Software 2.0” (Karpathy 2017) and, more recently, described prompting models in English as a new kind of programming (Karpathy 2025). I take a narrower and more testable position. I do not claim that English replaces programming languages. I claim that the unit a person writes is changing from code to a bundle of intent and checks, and that the environment a person works in is changing from an editor to a loop. If both hold, then the agentic loop is, in the plain historical sense, the next language and the next IDE.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
2. Background
The ladder. When FORTRAN appeared in 1957, its designers faced deep scepticism that machine-generated code could approach hand-written assembly; much of their effort went into the optimiser, precisely to win that argument (Backus 1978). They won, and the pattern repeated with every later level of abstraction.
Natural language as code. The idea of programming in English is old. Jean Sammet discussed it in 1966 (Sammet 1966); Edsger Dijkstra called it foolish in the late 1970s, arguing that the precision of formal notation is a feature, not a burden (Dijkstra, n.d.). Program synthesis research pursued the goal from specifications and examples for decades (Gulwani et al. 2017), with success in narrow domains.
Agents that code. Language models trained on code reached usable accuracy on small functions in 2021 (Chen et al. 2021). Since then, agents that read a repository, edit files, run tests and iterate have been evaluated on real GitHub issues (Jimenez et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024). The productivity evidence is mixed: a controlled experiment found developers 55.8% faster on a small, well-specified task with an AI pair programmer (Peng et al. 2023), while a randomised study of experienced open-source developers on their own mature repositories found them 19% slower with early-2025 tools (Becker et al. 2025).

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
3. A minimal definition
I define a program, in the agentic sense, as a tuple

P = (I,\; T,\; K,\; \Gamma),

where I is the intent, what is wanted, stated in words and examples; T is a set of executable checks (tests, types, properties, linters) that a candidate implementation must pass; K is the context, the repository and its conventions; and \Gamma is the set of tools and interfaces the agent may use, described as data in the sense of The Interface Is Data.
An agent A maps a program to code, c = A(P). A classical compiler is deterministic and preserves meaning by construction. An agent does neither. It is a stochastic compiler: its output can vary between runs, and it is correct only in the weak sense that

T(c) = \text{pass}.

Call the specification gap of P the set of behaviours that pass T but are not what I meant. The whole discipline of the new language is to make this gap small: by sharpening I, by strengthening T, and by having a person review what remains.



Figure 2. Schematic. The agent as a stochastic compiler. The program is the tuple of intent, checks, context and tools. The agent produces code, which is checked automatically and then reviewed by a person. Failed checks send the agent back; review refines the intent and strengthens the checks.


Under this definition, the concepts of the familiar toolchain map onto new ones.

Table 1. The toolchain, translated. My own mapping.


Today
In the agentic loop




Source file
Intent, examples and checks: (I, T)


Compiler
Agent: c = A(P), stochastic


Type checker
Tests, types and properties: T(c)


Standard library
Tools and interfaces: \Gamma


Build configuration
Repository context and conventions: K


Debugger
Decision log and execution trace of the agent


Code review
Review of intent first, then of the diff


Editor
Plan, diff and checks panes; typing as fallback

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
4. Four arguments
4.1 Historical. Every previous rung of the ladder was resisted on the grounds that generated output was slower, less precise or less trustworthy than what experts wrote by hand (Backus 1978). Each time, the generated output improved, the cost of writing by hand stayed the same, and the line crossed. Nothing in the current situation suggests the pattern has stopped; the objections raised today are the same three.
4.2 Structural. Brooks distinguished the essential complexity of software, deciding precisely what it must do, from its accidental complexity, the effort of expressing that decision in a particular language and toolset (Brooks 1987). Under the definition above, a person writes I and T, which carry the essential complexity, and the agent handles the expression, which is accidental. This is the division of labour every abstraction has aimed for, achieved at a higher level than before. Tests, long promoted as a design discipline (Beck 2002), become the main way to state that essential part.
4.3 Economic. The cost of producing a correct change has three parts: writing it, checking it, and understanding it later. Agentic coding drives the first towards zero and leaves the other two. A rational team will therefore spend its people where the cost remains, on intent, checks and review, which is exactly the shift from editor to loop that the thesis predicts. The IDE follows the work: when typing is no longer the bottleneck, an environment organised around typing is the wrong shape.
4.4 Empirical. Agents now resolve a meaningful share of real repository issues under controlled evaluation (Jimenez et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024), a task that requires reading context, editing several files and passing existing tests: the full loop of Figure 2, not autocomplete. The negative result of Becker et al. (2025) is important and I return to it in §6, but it measures an early tool generation, on large mature repositories, with developers who had little experience of the new way of working. That is close to measuring FORTRAN in 1957 with assembly experts.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
5. Predictions
A position paper should be falsifiable. If the thesis is right, the following should be observed in professional software over the next few years; if they are not, it is wrong.

H1. Authorship shifts. The share of merged changes whose code was primarily produced by an agent keeps rising in professional repositories, measurable from commit metadata and tool logs.
H2. Checks grow relative to code. In human-written lines, the ratio of tests, types and specifications to implementation rises.
H3. Review becomes the main human cost. Time spent reviewing and specifying exceeds time spent writing code, in the same teams that adopt agents.
H4. Gains follow the strength of checks. Productivity gains from agents are larger where T is strong (well-tested code with clear conventions) than where it is weak, other things equal. This is the most direct test of claim 3.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
6. Objections
Natural language is too imprecise (Dijkstra). This is right, and it is the most important objection. But the program in §3 is not prose alone. Its precision lives in T, in K and in review, as it always has in teams where a person states a need and an engineer implements it. The objection becomes a design rule: wherever precision matters, state it as a check, not as a sentence.
A stochastic compiler cannot be trusted. Deterministic compilers can be trusted because their meaning-preservation can be argued once. A stochastic compiler cannot; it must be checked every time. This raises the value of T and of review, and it means that for code where checks are weak and errors are costly, the old way should remain. The thesis predicts a shift in the default, not the end of hand-written code.
Developers are slower, not faster (Becker et al. 2025). If replications on strong-check repositories, with experienced users of current tools, continue to find slowdowns, H4 fails and so does much of this paper. I consider this the most likely way for me to be wrong.
Code is still the artefact that runs. Yes, as assembly still runs. The thesis does not say code disappears; it says it stops being the thing people mainly write. Like assembly, it remains the layer that can always be read, and to which the machine is held.
Literate programming tried this. Knuth argued that programs should be written for people first (Knuth 1984). Literate programming kept the person as the author of the code. The difference here is that the person is the author of the intent and the checks, and the code is derived.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
7. Conclusion
Every generation of programmers was told that the next level of abstraction was a toy, and each time the toy became the language. I have argued, on purpose without hedging, that the agentic loop is the next such level: the source becomes intent plus checks, the compiler becomes a stochastic agent held to those checks, and the IDE becomes a place to steer and review. The definition makes one consequence precise. The new language is exactly as rigorous as its checks, so the craft of programming does not disappear; it moves into specification, testing and judgement. Four predictions make the claim testable. I expect to be partly wrong. I would rather be wrong in a way that can be measured.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
Agentic Coding · Part 1 of 5 · Read the whole series
Abstract. Most of an AI agent’s calls to a large language model end in a multiple-choice pick: which tool, which argument, stop or continue. Zhu and colleagues ask whether these picks can be handed to a small decision model that answers in milliseconds, without losing task success. Their answer is yes, under three conditions: the decision model is tested inside the agent rather than on isolated questions, it is used only when its confidence clears a threshold fitted on the agent’s own runs, and it is trained on the states the agent actually reaches, including after its own mistakes. Under these conditions, an open 4B model made customer-service agents 86.3% cheaper and 2.5 times faster with no detectable loss of success. The gains were small in coding agents, and the method failed badly on a rule the model had never seen, until thresholds were refitted. I argue that this is the missing piece of Fast AI: a fast path at the level of single choices, which knows when it is unsure and learns its habits from the slow path.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
1. The question
In Fast AI I argued that automation should learn slowly, once, and act fast every time, keeping the large model for the exceptions. The essay left one practical question open: inside a running agent, how do you know which steps are routine, and what answers them if not the large model?
The JevAgentHarness paper addresses exactly this. Its starting observation is simple. Watch an agent work and count what it decides. A customer asks to cancel an order; the agent must choose to look up the order, cancel it, or ask the customer first; then which order; then which reason from a fixed list; then whether the task is done. Each of these is a call to a large language model that reads the whole context and writes its answer token by token, in seconds. Yet almost every one ends in picking one item from a list the harness already knows.
The authors identify eight such decision points in one step of an agent loop: three that choose what the agent does (the tool, its arguments, or the next action) and five that control the loop (write memory, read memory, reflect after a failure, stop, or route the step to a cheaper model). Their research question is how a harness can delegate these choices “to a fast, cheap decision model when the model is reliable, so that agentic tasks become faster and cheaper with little loss of success.”



Figure 1. Schematic. Today the large model makes every choice of the loop. With a decision model, the routine choices are answered in milliseconds, and the large model is called only where the decision model is unsure.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
2. Background: decision models
Decision models are a new class of model built for this kind of choice. Given a context and a question with fixed options, they return a probability for each option instead of generating text. The best known is Jev, released by TypeSafe in September 2026 and presented as a “System One” model, after Daniel Kahneman’s fast, intuitive mode of thinking (TypeSafe announcement). Its weights and size are not public. In one episode recorded by Zhu and colleagues, a call to Jev took 28% of an LLM call’s time and 2.6% of its price; the project repository estimates about 0.15 s and $0.0001 for a typical coding-agent state.
Open counterparts appeared within weeks, among them Intern-Decision, StartLux-Decision and OpenJev. So did the first independent evaluations, which are worth reading before trusting any of these models. As a cheap judge, Jev detected alignment failures such as sycophancy and prompt injection about as well as a reference LLM scorer, at a fraction of the cost (Guo et al., 2026). As a rubric judge, it was found “cheaper, faster, and wrong in the same places” as LLMs (Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026). Adversarial tests show that small edits to a question can flip its typed answers (JevAdvBench), and one study reports that swapping the order of “yes” and “no” changes many of its answers (arXiv 2610.00346).
The idea itself is older than these models. A classifier that may abstain when unsure is known as selective classification (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017); one that hands cases to an expert is learning to defer (Mozannar and Sontag, 2020). Routers and cascades such as FrugalGPT and RouteLLM apply it to whole requests, and agents that think “fast and slow”, such as SwiftSage or the Talker-Reasoner architecture, apply it to whole steps. What is new in JevAgentHarness is the grain: one typed choice at a time, inside the agent, with a threshold per kind of choice.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
3. The approach
The paper has three parts, one for each condition the authors believe a decision model needs to be useful.
A benchmark at three levels. AgentDecisionBench tests decision models on isolated questions (level 1), at each step of recorded agent runs, where answers are scored but not executed (level 2), and in control of a running agent, where every choice changes what comes next (level 3). Because public benchmarks only check the end of a run, the authors built DecisionGym, a simulated customer-service desk in the style of τ-bench, which knows the acceptable next steps at every reachable state, including after detours. Each task offers 68 tools in shuffled order, among them 31 near-duplicates of the core tools.
A harness that asks, then decides whether to trust. JevAgentHarness plugs into existing harnesses such as mini-SWE-agent or the pi terminal agent through their hooks. At each routine choice, it asks the decision model a typed multiple-choice question: tools, fixed-list or yes/no argument values, or spans to copy from the context. In the main mode, the cascade, the answer is used only when the decision model’s confidence c clears a threshold. Otherwise the large model decides as usual. The paper derives the threshold from a simple cost argument: delegating is worth it when

c \;\ge\; q_L - \frac{\Delta C}{V},

where q_L is how often the large model gets this choice right, \Delta C the price of the saved call and V the cost of a wrong choice. The small model may be slightly less accurate than the large one, as long as the saving covers the extra risk. In practice, the agent first runs on separate tasks while the decision model answers silently (shadow mode), and the threshold is fitted on these runs for each decision point. With Jev and Gemini 3.5 Flash, the fitted thresholds were 1.00 for tools and 0.99 for arguments: only near-certain answers are used.



Figure 2. The threshold rule of Zhu and colleagues, with illustrative values of my own. When a call costs little against what a wrong choice costs, the threshold sits just under the large model’s own accuracy.


A model trained on the agent’s own states. AgentDecision-4B is Qwen3-4B with a LoRA adapter. The harness ran 587 training tasks and recorded every decision state, 15,694 in all. To include states after errors, a scripted policy repeated mistakes seen during development, an idea from imitation learning (Ross et al., 2011), so that 30.9% of the states follow a mistake. Jev’s probabilities served as soft labels, mixed with the correct answer, under a loss that also keeps the probabilities calibrated. A second stage of reinforcement learning inside the agent loop rewarded success with fewer LLM calls.
The protocol is careful: the models, tasks and tests were registered before the main runs, each delegation was tested alone for non-inferiority (less than 3 points of success lost, at the 5% level, with a correction for multiple tests), and only then were the passing delegations combined and tested on new tasks.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
4. Findings

4.1 Isolated scores misrank decision models
On isolated questions, the models were within about 5 points of each other. Inside a running agent, their task success spread over 57 points. StartLux-9B, the most accurate on isolated tool choice at 92.2%, solved 69.5% of tasks. AgentDecision-4B, at 89.3%, solved 91.5%. The difference lies in the hard states, such as the moments when the right move is to ask the customer before an irreversible action: there, AgentDecision-4B answered 67.4% correctly and Jev 58.3%. Accuracy on recorded agent steps ranked the models nearly as task success did (Kendall correlation 0.84).



Figure 3. Accuracy on isolated questions against tasks solved when the model makes the agent’s tool choices, on shifted customer-service tasks. Data from Zhu et al., Figure 4b.




4.2 A fitted threshold protects success
With a fitted threshold, Jev made 27.2% of the tool choices and 20.8% of the argument choices, cutting cost by 14.2% without changing the outcome of any of 500 tasks. Without a threshold, letting Jev make every tool choice lost 19.0 points of success; a fixed threshold of 0.5 lost 21.5. The threshold, not the model, is what makes delegation safe.


4.3 Training on the agent’s own states works
Supervised training on the agent’s own states raised the 4B model from 13.5% to 96.0% of shifted tasks solved, for 2.2 GPU-hours. The same recipe raised StartLux-4B from 49.0% to 98.0%. The reinforcement-learning stage added no measurable gain, which the authors report plainly. The student beat its teacher: Jev solved 82.0% of the same tasks. On one L4 graphics card, AgentDecision-4B answered in a median of 31 ms, against 809 ms for a call to Gemini 3.5 Flash.



Figure 4. Tasks solved on shifted customer-service tasks, with different decision models making the agent’s tool choices. Data from Zhu et al., Table 3.




4.4 The gains depend on how much the choices repeat



Figure 5. LLM cost saved, with the change in task success against the large model alone, in four settings. Data from Zhu et al., Tables 1 and 2.



Customer service. On 500 new tasks, AgentDecision-4B on its own graphics card made 99.9% of the tool choices and 75.0% of the argument choices, saving 4.5 LLM calls per task: 86.3% cheaper, 2.5 times faster, success within half a point of the large model alone.
Text games. On ALFWorld, a 4B model trained on the game’s states made the agent 89.0% cheaper and about twice as fast, with higher success, and kept these gains in unseen rooms.
Coding agents. Actions are free text, so the decision model could only choose which LLM writes each step. Savings were 7.0–10.5%, and success varied by harness.



4.5 Fast models fail confidently on new rules
On harder tasks with a cancellation rule no model was trained on, AgentDecision-4B made most cancel-or-ship choices but got only 81.6% of them right, and the agent solved 3.0% of the tasks, against 88.0% for the large model alone. Refitting the threshold restored success; retraining on the rule raised the model’s accuracy from 76.5% to 95.3%. In the same vein, all 34 of Jev’s failed tasks began with an irreversible wrong tool choice, usually cancelling where the agent should have asked.

title: The Junior Colleague
section: 5. Analysis: what this means for Fast AI
text:
5. Analysis: what this means for Fast AI
Fast AI proposed a split: deep networks perceive, a knowledge graph remembers, trees decide, and the agentic loop is kept for the exceptions. The paper does not test this architecture, but its results bear on it in five ways.
Decision models fill the gap between trees and the large model. Gradient-boosted trees remain my choice when a decision rests on structured features. But many choices in a process come as text: a customer message, a chat history, a ticket. These used to fall to the large model by default. A small decision model now handles them in milliseconds, with a probability attached.
“Knowing when unsure” becomes an engineering step. Fast AI required every fast model to know when to hand over, without saying how. The paper’s answer is concrete: run in shadow mode, measure, fit one threshold per kind of choice, refit when something changes. Finding 4.2 shows this step matters more than the choice of model.
The habit loop is the training loop. Finding 4.3 is the habit-forming step of Fast AI, made measurable. The slow, expensive teachers, Jev and the large model, label the agent’s own experience once. The fast student learns the habits of this agent in this domain, including how to recover from its own errors. Logged deferrals become the next round of training data.



Figure 6. Fast AI with a decision model. Each listed choice goes to a small decision model. Above its threshold, it decides; below, the large model, an agent or a person does. The logs, including the agent’s mistakes, are used to retrain the model and refit the thresholds, which are tested in shadow mode before they are trusted.


The knowledge graph still matters, perhaps more. A decision model is only as good as its options, and Finding 4.5 shows what happens when the rules change under it. In a well-built system, the graph supplies the options (which tools apply to this supplier, which approvers are valid for this amount) and holds the rules in a form a person can read and correct. When a rule changes, the change is made once in the graph, and the thresholds are refitted. Habits in weights are fast; habits in a graph are auditable. A serious system needs both.
It fits the local ecosystem. A 4B model on one graphics card is the kind of small specialist I described in An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle. NVIDIA researchers make the same argument for agents in general: most of what agents do is narrow and repetitive, and small models can do it more economically (Belcak et al., 2025). Decision models push this furthest, because picking an option is far narrower than writing.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
6. Limits and open questions
The paper is careful about its limits, and they shape how far its results can be carried.

External validity. All tasks are in English, most runs use Gemini models, and the most striking numbers come from the authors’ own environment, DecisionGym. Independent replication on real workloads is the next step.
Fitted to one agent. Thresholds and trained models are fitted to one agent’s runs. A new agent, new tools or a new task family call for refitting and, for the best accuracy, retraining.
Silent drift. Finding 4.5 shows that confidence does not drop on its own when rules change. The authors suggest tracking the share of answers above the threshold; I would add the shape-based monitoring of What a Quiet Screen Cannot See.
Irreversible actions. A confident wrong choice at an irreversible step ends the task. The authors warn that a decision-model guard should never be the only control on such an action, and that adapters should not be used as security boundaries.
Statistics. The main tests show that success drops by less than 3 points; showing equal success would need an equivalence test. The authors did not compare against learned routers such as RouteLLM on the same tasks.
Licence. The trained weights are released under a non-commercial licence, partly because they are trained on outputs of a proprietary model.

Two questions seem open to me. First, how much of the gain survives when the options themselves must be discovered, rather than listed by the harness? Second, can the threshold and the knowledge graph be kept in step automatically, so that a rule change in the graph triggers refitting before it triggers failures?

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
7. Conclusion
The large model was never meant to answer “which of these three tools?” ten thousand times a day. It was meant to handle what is new, and to teach.
JevAgentHarness shows a careful way to arrange this: ask a small decision model first, trust it only above a threshold fitted on your own runs, test it on your own work rather than on a leaderboard, and train it on the states your agent really reaches, mistakes included. When the choices repeat, the result is an agent several times faster and far cheaper, with no detectable loss of success. When the world changes, the same discipline of shadow mode, refitting and retraining is what keeps it safe.
That is a junior colleague in the best sense: fast on the routine, honest about what they do not know, and getting better every month from what the seniors decide. It is also Fast AI, one choice at a time.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
Evenings with Physics · Part 2 of 4 · Read the whole series
In short. A physics paper about how structure appears out of complete disorder made me ask a question I could actually test: while an AI image generator turns noise into a picture, where does the picture’s information live, in the inside of a region or on its border? I ran the experiment in one evening, on two CPU cores, with an AI as lab partner. Finished images follow an area law: information lives on borders. But on the way, the big decisions are made across the whole image first, and only later settle onto the edges. I also found a way to measure this inside any image generator using nothing but its ability to remove noise, and checked it against exact answers. None of this is my field. The part I want to stress is how it was possible at all.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
section: 1. It must be simpler than this
text:
1. It must be simpler than this
Recently I wrote about reading a physics paper I could not follow: Holograms and Standard Models, by Miyashita, Sekino and Susskind. My first reaction was simple. Something is wrong here. It must be easier. I believe the universe is fundamentally simple.
That essay ended in philosophy. Grains inside grains, nothing creating everything, and the idea that the meaning is in the middle.
This one ends in an experiment.
I am a software architect, not a physicist. But I kept coming back to one idea from that paper, and one evening I asked a different question: could I actually test something? Not about the universe. About the AI systems I work with every day.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
2. The surface knows everything
The idea that stuck is the holographic principle. In the 1970s, Bekenstein and Hawking found that the information a black hole can hold depends on the area of its surface, not on its volume. Double its size and its information grows four times, not eight.
Physicists found the same pattern elsewhere. In many systems, the information shared between a region and everything around it grows with the region’s boundary. They call it an area law. When it grows with the region’s size instead, it is a volume law.
Susskind and his colleagues go further. They build a small world of particles and forces from a system at infinite temperature, the state of maximum disorder, the closest thing to “nothing” physics allows. Structure from nothing, organised on a surface.
I could not check their mathematics. But their question felt general: when structure appears out of complete disorder, where does its information live?

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
section: 3. A machine that builds structure from disorder
text:
3. A machine that builds structure from disorder
Then I realised I already knew a machine that builds structure from disorder.
Image generators like Stable Diffusion are diffusion models. They start from pure random noise, the same maximum-disorder state, and remove the noise step by step until an image appears. A face, a cat, a handwritten digit.
The universe gives us one run, seen from inside, mostly through a horizon. A diffusion model gives us as many runs as we want, and we can stop it at any moment and look.
So the question became concrete. While an image forms out of noise, does the information shared between a patch of the image and the rest of it grow with the patch’s border, or with its size? Area or volume? And does that change along the way?

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
4. What I measured
The measurement is simple to state. Take a square patch of an image. Ask how much knowing the rest of the image tells you about that patch. Physicists call this mutual information. Then make the patch bigger and watch how that number grows.
If it grows like the border of the patch, it is an area law. If it grows like the number of pixels inside, it is a volume law. I summarise the growth with one number, β, from

I(L) \propto L^{\beta},

where L is the side of the patch in pixels: β close to 1 means area law, close to 2 means volume law.
I did not use a giant neural network. I used something I could compute exactly: a statistical model of handwritten digits (the classic MNIST dataset) built from 40 simple pieces, four per digit. It learns real structure; on images it has never seen, it is far better than a simple model. And for this kind of model, every stage between noise and finished image can be calculated precisely, with no training noise and no guessing.
The most important part is the comparison. For every measurement I also built a control: a much simpler model that has exactly the same correlations between pixels but none of the real structure. No strokes, no digits, just smooth statistical blur. Whatever the real model does that the control does not, comes from actual structure. Without that control, I would have fooled myself at least twice.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
5. What I found
Finished digits follow an area law. At the end of generation, β is 1.07. The information a patch shares with the rest of the image grows with its border.
But on the way, something else happens. In the noisy early phase, the real model carries up to 2.4 times more shared information than the control, and that extra information grows more like the size of the patch than its border. As the image sharpens, the extra information moves toward the borders, and the two curves meet (Figure 1).



Figure 1. Left: digits generated by the learned model. Right: the scaling exponent β along the generation path, from heavy noise (left) to finished image (right). The real model (blue) carries extra, bulk-like information in the noisy phase, well above the control with the same pixel correlations (orange). Both converge to an area law, β = 1.07 for finished digits.


Here is how I read it. Early on, the model is deciding the big things: which digit, roughly where, which way it leans. That is a fact about the whole image, and every pixel carries a little evidence about it, so it scales with size. Later, the model draws the details: strokes, edges, where black meets white. Those are local, and they live on borders.
Or, in one line: structure is decided in the bulk and written on the boundary.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
6. What did not work
I expected a sudden switch, like water turning to ice, at one precise moment. A first coarse run seemed to show one. When I repeated it with eleven noise levels and three independent runs, the jump disappeared. The change is smooth (Figure 2). The “sudden switch” was noise in a single run.



Figure 2. The same measurement on a fine grid of noise levels, repeated three times with independent model fits and samples (bars: ±2 standard deviations). a. The total information converges smoothly to an area law; there is no sudden jump. b. The part that comes from real structure, beyond the control, starts close to a volume law and moves toward an area law as the image sharpens.


I keep it in the story because it is exactly the kind of mistake that is easy to publish and hard to take back.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
7. What it does not show
I asked for a tough review of my own results, the kind a referee would write. Here is what holds up less well than I would like.

The area law alone is not surprising. Any image whose pixels mostly correlate with their neighbours gives an area law. Physicists have known this for years. The new part is not the final area law but the extra structure and how it moves from bulk to boundary.
It describes the data, not the network. Because I computed everything exactly, the results describe what noisy digits look like at each stage, which is the same for any perfect generator. To say how real neural networks behave, I need to test a trained one.
The images are tiny. At 28×28 pixels I can only compare patches from 2 to 12 pixels wide. That is less than one order of magnitude, and the blank border of each digit distorts larger patches.
The physics is an analogy. A black hole’s surface and the border of an image patch are not the same thing. The parallel is suggestive, and testable, but it is not a proof of anything about the universe.

None of this makes the work worthless. It tells me exactly what to do next.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
8. Seeing inside any generator
The second limitation bothered me most. My exact method only works on simple models. Real generators, the ones people actually use, are giant neural networks where nothing can be computed exactly.
Then I came across a result from information theory, from 2005, by Guo, Shamai and Verdú. It links information to how hard it is to remove noise. Applied to my question, it says something I find beautiful:

The information a patch shares with the rest of the image equals how much seeing the rest helps you clean up that patch, added up over all noise levels.

In symbols, with A the patch, B the rest of the image and \text{mmse} the error of the best possible denoiser at a given signal-to-noise ratio \gamma:

I(A;B) = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\text{snr}} \Big[\, \text{mmse}_A(\gamma) + \text{mmse}_B(\gamma) - \text{mmse}_{A \cup B}(\gamma) \,\Big]\, d\gamma

That matters because cleaning up noise is exactly what a diffusion model is trained to do. So in principle you could measure the information map of any generator just by asking it to denoise a patch twice: once seeing only the patch, once seeing the whole image.
I tested this on my digit model, where I already knew the exact answer. The two routes agree, with a median difference of 3% across 32 comparisons (patch sizes from 2 to 12 pixels, noise levels from heavy to light). The largest difference was 14%, on one very small, very noisy patch (Figure 3).



Figure 3. Information measured from denoising errors alone (vertical) against the exact value (horizontal), for 32 combinations of patch size and noise level. Points on the dashed line agree perfectly. The median difference is 3.1%.


This is the part I find most valuable. The exact calculations become a ground truth to check a method that can scale to real models. The next step is to run it on a trained neural network. That needs a model that can denoise with part of the image hidden, which many image generators already can.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
section: 9. You don’t need a big machine
text:
9. You don’t need a big machine
Everything in this essay ran on two CPU cores. No GPU, no cloud cluster, no downloaded giant model. The longest run took about seven minutes.
At one point I was told the next step needed a GPU. I pushed back: why should a question need a big machine? It turned out the honest answer was that only one specific claim needs it, the one about trained neural networks. Everything else, the exact calculations, the controls, the repeated runs, fits on a laptop. Some of the best physics ever done was tabletop physics. A well-controlled small experiment beats a sloppy big one.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
section: 10. A lab partner, not an oracle
text:
10. A lab partner, not an oracle
I should be transparent about how this was done. I did it in one evening with Claude, Anthropic’s AI, as a lab partner. I brought the questions and the stubbornness; it wrote and ran the code, searched the literature, and, importantly, reviewed the results harshly when I asked it to. It also caught its own mistakes: a model that looked better than it was, a chart label that overstated a result, a “sudden transition” that was not there.
Look back at the path of this essay and count the steps that would have stopped me alone:

From a feeling to a measurable question. “It must be simpler” is not a hypothesis. Turning it into “does mutual information scale with the border or the size, and does that change along the generation path?” took a conversation, not a degree.
From a question to code that runs. Exact mutual information for a 784-pixel mixture model, Monte Carlo estimates with error bars, a fair control. Each is a week of reading for an outsider. Here, each was a script I could read, run and question within minutes.
From a result to a result I trust. The control model, the three independent runs, the fine grid of noise levels: these exist because I kept asking “how would I fool myself here?”, and the answers came back as experiments, not opinions.
From a dead end to a way forward. The method that works on real generators comes from a 2005 information-theory paper I had never heard of. Finding it, understanding what it says about my question, and testing it against the exact values all happened in the same evening.
From a claim to a smaller, honest claim. The harsh review took the area law off its pedestal and left the more interesting part standing. The GPU question turned “this needs a big machine” into “only this one claim does”.

None of these steps is new science on its own. What is new, for me, is that they can follow each other at the speed of curiosity. The distance between “I wonder whether…” and “here is the plot, here is the control, here is why it might be wrong” used to be months, and for someone outside the field it was usually infinite. That evening it was hours.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
11. Innovation is in the asking
This is the part of AI I find most interesting. Not that it answers, but that it lets someone like me ask properly: run the experiment, check it, and throw away what does not hold.
It is tempting to say that AI will produce new ideas by itself. I do not think that is what happened here. The question came from me, reading a paper I could not follow and refusing to let it go. The direction changed three times because of judgement calls: insist on a control, distrust a jump that looked too good, refuse to accept that a question needs a big machine. What the AI removed was the cost of each step in between. When trying an idea costs minutes instead of weeks, you try more of them, you kill the bad ones sooner, and the good ones get pushed further than you would ever have pushed them alone.
That also changes what rigour means for an outsider. The danger of a fast partner is that you go fast in the wrong direction, and a confident AI can make a wrong result look finished. The defence is the same as in any lab: controls, repeated runs, a referee who is paid to be unkind, and everything published so that others can check. The AI can play the referee too, if you ask it to. You have to ask.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
12. A very good middle
I started with a feeling: the universe must be simpler than that paper. I still believe it. But I see now that simple does not mean easy, and it does not mean finished.
In my last essay I wrote that “from nothing to nothing” forgets the middle, and that the middle is everything. This experiment is a small version of that idea. A machine starts from noise, from nothing. It ends with a digit, a finished thing. And in between, there is a moment where the big decisions are made everywhere at once, before they settle quietly onto the edges.
I don’t know if the universe works like that. I do know that a question asked on a quiet evening can become something you can measure. That is not the end of anything. It is a very good middle.

title: Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary
text:
13. Try it yourself
Everything is open. You can rerun every number and every figure in this essay on an ordinary laptop in about half an hour.

Code and results: download as a zip, or browse on GitHub. It contains all scripts, the result files, the figures, and a run_all.sh that reproduces everything. The only thing to download is the MNIST dataset (about 11 MB); the README gives the link. MIT licence.
Working paper: From Noise to Boundaries: Area-Law Information Scaling Along the Diffusion Path, a four-page technical version with the equations and references.
Requirements: Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib. No GPU.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
Essay, October 2026. A follow-up to Show What Changed, Not the Data. The simulation code is here: sim.py, figs.py.
In short. My last essay argued that a dashboard should show only how our understanding of a system has changed, so that most weeks it is empty. A reader pointed out the weak spot: if something goes wrong in a place our understanding does not cover, the screen stays quiet while the system fails. He is right, and this essay takes the objection seriously. An empty dashboard can mean two different things, nothing changed or something changed where we are not looking, and the dashboard alone cannot tell them apart. But the data can. Every summary leaves something unexplained, and when the world changes in a direction the summary does not cover, that leftover part grows. Watching it costs very little, and it turns a silent blind spot into a warning.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
1. The objection
After I published the first essay, a reader named Ronald wrote a comment that I have been thinking about since. He liked the idea and compared it to how the brain works: it does not process everything it receives, it predicts what should happen and reacts only to the difference. An empty dashboard, he said, is like a well-adapted organism with nothing to react to.
Then he added the caveat. The dashboard has a built-in blind spot. If something goes wrong outside what the shape describes, the screen stays silent while the system fails without a sound.
I had mentioned this limit at the end of the paper, in one paragraph. That was not enough. The whole proposal rests on one promise: if the screen is empty, you can look away. If an empty screen can also mean “something is breaking where I cannot see”, then the promise is broken, and the old crowded dashboard starts to look safer. So the question deserves a full answer: when can we trust silence?

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
2. Two silences
Imagine two weeks in which the dashboard shows nothing.
In the first week, nothing changed. The system behaved as our shape (our compact description of how it works) said it would. Silence is good news.
In the second week, something did change, but in a direction the shape does not describe. Perhaps one type of device became slow, and the shape does not track devices. The shape is recomputed, it looks the same as last week, the difference is zero, and the screen is empty. Silence is now bad news, and it looks exactly like the good news.
In the first essay I added a heartbeat: a weekly line saying “shape checked on this week’s data, no material change.” It solves a real problem. Without it, a broken pipeline and a healthy system both produce an empty screen. But the heartbeat only proves that the system is checking. It does not prove that the system can see the change that matters. In the second week, the heartbeat is sent, it is true, and it is useless.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
section: 3. The geometry of a blind spot
text:
3. The geometry of a blind spot
It helps to picture this. The shape is a small set of numbers: for example the speed of each agent in each language, after removing the effect of request length and the daily ups and downs of the shared servers. Think of each number as one direction in which the system can move. Together, these directions form the space that the shape describes.
Any real change in the system is an arrow. Part of that arrow points along the directions the shape describes; that part moves the shape and reaches the dashboard. The rest points elsewhere; it moves nothing the shape measures, so the difference of shapes does not see it at all (Figure 1).



Figure 1. A change in the system splits into two parts. The part along what the shape describes moves the shape card and can reach the dashboard. The part outside it is invisible, however large. A large real change can still show only a small shadow on the dashboard, too small to report.


Mathematicians call the visible part a projection. The dashboard of the first essay sees only the projection of each change onto the shape. This is not a flaw of one dashboard; it is true of every model, every summary and every set of indicators. You can only report a change in the words you have. A thermometer cannot tell you that the room is on fire if the fire has not yet warmed the air near it.
The danger is not only that some changes are invisible. It is that the shape will often explain them away. If a change looks, from inside the shape, like something the shape already expects, such as noise or a known swing, the shape will absorb it into that category without complaint.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
4. The setup
To see how this happens, I reused the simulated AI copilot from the first essay: five agents (search, code, summarise, translate, email), four languages (English, German, French, Italian), request lengths, slow growth, quiet weekends, and response times that rise and fall each day for everyone because the servers are shared. Over 12 weeks the simulation produces about 2.2 million requests.
One thing is new. Each request now also records three fields the shape card does not use: the device (web browser, desktop app or iOS app), the region and the customer’s plan. This is realistic. Telemetry usually records far more fields than any summary uses.
The shape card is the same as before: the speed of each agent in each language, after removing the effect of request length and the shared daily swings. It learns the length rule correctly (exponent 0.50, the value used to create the data) and it is quiet for seven weeks, as it should be.
Then, on the Wednesday of week 8, requests from the iOS app become 15% slower, for every agent and every language. Perhaps an app update changed how requests are packed. iOS is 15% of all traffic.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
5. Why the shape stays quiet
The shape card never moves. Over the twelve weeks, the largest change in any of its numbers is 2.6% from one week to the next, and 2.5% compared with the reference weeks. The materiality line is 5%. The dashboard is empty for all twelve weeks, and twelve heartbeats report “no material change” (Figure 2).
The reason is instructive. The slowdown hits every agent and every language equally, because iOS users are spread evenly across them. So the relative speeds that the shape card tracks do not change at all. What does change is the overall level: on average, all requests are about 2% slower. But the shape was built to treat changes in the overall level as server swings, because the servers really do swing, by about 5% from day to day. A step of 2% inside daily swings of 5% looks like one more swing. Look at the top panel of Figure 2: the 7-day average wandered just as much in weeks 3 and 4, when nothing was wrong.



Figure 2. Top: the shared daily level, which the shape treats as server swings. The iOS slowdown adds a step of about 2% from day 51, inside daily swings of about 5%. It is indistinguishable from earlier wandering. Bottom: the dashboard. The largest change in the shape card never comes close to the 5% line.


This is the worst kind of blind spot. The shape does not ignore the problem. It explains it, with full confidence and the wrong explanation. A 15% slowdown for one in seven users becomes “the servers had a slightly slow fortnight”.
The fourth caution of the first essay, comparing against a fixed reference and not only against last week, does not help here either. That caution catches slow changes along the directions the shape describes. This change is not slow; it is sideways.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
6. The leftover part
The way out comes from an idea that was already at the centre of the first essay. The shortest description of a set of data has two parts:

\text{data} = \text{rule} + \text{exceptions}

The shape is the rule. The exceptions are everything the rule does not explain: for each small group of requests, the gap between the speed the shape predicts and the speed that was actually measured.
When the shape is right, the exceptions are pure noise. They have a typical size, which we can measure in quiet weeks, and they have no structure: you cannot predict them from anything.
When the world changes in a direction the shape does not describe, the change has to go somewhere. It cannot go into the shape, so it goes into the exceptions. In the language of Figure 1, the unseen part of the arrow is not lost; it lands in the leftover part. The exceptions get bigger, and they start to have a pattern.
So the shape needs a second, very simple monitor next to the dashboard. It asks two questions each week.

Are the exceptions bigger than usual? If the rule still holds, the leftover part should be as large as it was in quiet weeks, no larger.
Can anything explain them? For each recorded field that the shape does not use, check how much of the exceptions it explains. If the shape still holds, the answer should be: almost nothing.

The first question tells us that the shape is wearing out. The second tells us where.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
7. What the exceptions show
Figure 3 shows the first question in the simulation. The size of the exceptions is measured relative to the first six weeks, so 1 means “usual”. For seven weeks it stays within about 1% of 1. In week 8, it jumps to 1.18, then settles between 1.30 and 1.37. With a materiality line at +10%, the monitor raises a notice at the end of week 8, five days after the problem began. The shape card, for the same weeks, still says nothing has changed.



Figure 3. The size of the exceptions, relative to the first six weeks. It stays at 1 until the iOS problem starts, then crosses the +10% line at the end of week 8. The dashed line shows what happens once the shape learns device type: the exceptions return to their usual size.


There is something important here. This first check does not need the device field at all. It only needs to know that the rule now explains the data less well than it used to. Even if the device were never recorded, we would know that the shape no longer fits, without knowing why. That alone is worth a lot: it changes the heartbeat from “no change” to “no change in the shape, but the shape fits worse than usual”. That is a very different message, and a much more honest one.
Figure 4 shows the second question. Before the problem, the device field explains only 1 to 2% of the exceptions. That small part is real: iOS requests were always about 3% slower, a constant difference the shape never learned. After week 8, the device field explains 18 to 19% of the exceptions. Region and plan stay below 1% throughout.



Figure 4. How much of the exceptions each recorded field explains. Device type jumps from 1–2% to almost 20% when the iOS problem starts. Region and plan stay close to zero. The monitor does not only say that something is wrong; it says where to look.


So the notice can say something precise: the shape fits worse than usual, and most of what it cannot explain is linked to device type; iOS requests are about 15% slower than the shape expects. That is almost the full diagnosis, found by a monitor that has no idea what an iOS app is.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
8. The shape learns
What happens next is the loop from the first essay: summarise, look at what the rule misses, summarise again. The notice tells us the shape is missing a dimension. So we add it: the shape card gains two numbers, the speed of the desktop app and of the iOS app relative to the web.
With those two numbers, the shape learns that iOS was about 3% slower than the web before week 8 and about 18% slower after, which matches the 15% slowdown we hid. The exceptions return to their usual size (the dashed line in Figure 3). The screen becomes quiet again, and this time the silence is justified.
This is how a shape should grow: not by adding every field “just in case”, which brings back the crowded dashboard and the curve with too many terms, but by adding a dimension when the exceptions prove that it is needed. The leftover part is not waste. It is where the next rule comes from. Kepler gave up circular orbits because of an eight-arcminute gap in the orbit of Mars that circles could not explain.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
section: 9. Predictive coding has the same problem
text:
9. Predictive coding has the same problem
Ronald’s comparison with the brain is a good one, and it goes further than he said. A well-known theory in neuroscience, predictive coding, proposes that the brain constantly predicts what its senses will report, and passes on mainly the difference between prediction and reality. This is exactly a dashboard of differences. And the brain has exactly the same blind spot.
The most famous demonstration is an experiment by Simons and Chabris. Viewers are asked to count the passes in a video of people throwing a basketball. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walks through the scene. Roughly half of the viewers do not notice the gorilla at all. They were not looking in the wrong place; the gorilla walked through the middle of the screen. Their model of the task simply had no slot for gorillas.
So how does the brain survive in a world full of gorillas? One influential answer, from Yu and Dayan, is that the brain tracks two kinds of uncertainty. Expected uncertainty is the normal noise of a familiar situation: we know the world is a bit unpredictable and we do not react to every small surprise. Unexpected uncertainty is when surprises become more frequent or larger than our model says they should be. That is the signal that the model itself is wrong, and it is thought to trigger a reset: attention widens, learning speeds up, old rules are questioned.
This is the exception monitor. The brain does not only watch what differs from its prediction. It watches how much it is being surprised overall, compared with how much it expects to be. When surprise rises above its usual level, the brain stops trusting its model and starts looking around. A dashboard should do the same.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
10. Changes that leave no trace
The exception monitor has a limit too, and it is better to say it plainly. It sees changes that leave a trace in the data, even in fields the shape does not use. It cannot see changes that leave no trace in any data at all.
Suppose the copilot’s answers in Italian slowly get worse, less accurate and less useful, while staying exactly as fast. Speed telemetry will never show it. No shape, no exception and no field will move, because nothing we record is affected. The only places this shows up are people: a user who stops using the copilot, a colleague in Milan who mentions it over coffee, an engineer who reads twenty Italian answers one afternoon.
So there are three kinds of change, and each needs a different watcher (Figure 5).



Figure 5. Three kinds of change and who can see them. Changes in what the shape describes reach the dashboard. Changes elsewhere in the data reach the exception monitor. Changes that leave no record can only be seen by people.



Changes inside the shape reach the dashboard. This is what the first essay was about.
Changes in the data but outside the shape reach the exception monitor. This is what this essay adds.
Changes outside the data reach no machine. They need people who regularly look at the real thing: read the answers, visit the shop floor, talk to the users.

The third circle is not a footnote. In 1983, Lisanne Bainbridge described the “ironies of automation”: the more reliable an automatic system becomes, the less often people practise the skills they need on the day it fails. A quiet dashboard makes this worse, because it removes the daily contact with the system that used to keep people’s intuition alive. If we take away the crowded screen, we must give back that contact in a deliberate form: a regular, unhurried look at raw cases, chosen at random, by people whose job is to notice what nobody asked them to look for.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
section: 11. Proving that the system can still see
text:
11. Proving that the system can still see
There is one more trap. Even a good exception monitor can break silently. A pipeline can stop filling a field; a threshold can be set too high after a busy month; a model can be retrained in a way that hides the exceptions inside the rule. Each of these produces a quiet screen.
Engineers already know how to deal with this in other fields. Fire alarms are tested. Pilots train in simulators on failures they hope never to see. In large software systems, chaos engineering deliberately breaks things in production, in small and controlled ways, to check that the monitoring notices.
The same idea works here. From time to time, inject a small, known, artificial change into a copy of the data: make one slice of synthetic requests slower, along a dimension the shape does not track. Then check that the exception monitor notices, and how fast. If it does not, the silence of the following weeks means nothing. If it does, we have evidence, not just hope, that the system can still see.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
12. A better heartbeat
Put together, the weekly heartbeat becomes a short, honest report of what was checked and how well:

Week 12. Shape checked on this week’s data: no material change. Exceptions: usual size; no recorded field explains them. Last drill: injected slowdown on a hidden slice, caught after 4 days. Last human review of raw cases: 3 weeks ago.

Each line answers a different doubt. The first says that our understanding still holds. The second says that it still fits: nothing is hiding in the leftover part. The third says that the watcher can still see. The fourth says when a person last looked at the world directly, outside every model.
This is still a very small amount to read: four lines a week instead of forty tiles a day. But now the silence carries information. It says not only “nothing changed”, but “nothing changed that we could have seen, here is how much we could see, and here is when we last checked the rest”.

title: What a Quiet Screen Cannot See
text:
13. Conclusion
The objection to the first essay was right: a system that only watches its own picture of the world cannot see what lies outside that picture, and it will often explain away what it cannot see. More tiles are not the answer; a crowded screen has blind spots too, it just hides them under noise.
The answer is to watch the part of the data the picture cannot explain. When the world moves sideways, away from what our model describes, the exceptions grow and take on a pattern long before anyone thinks of adding a new chart. Watching them is cheap, it needs no knowledge of what might go wrong, and it tells us both that our understanding has stopped fitting and roughly where.
And for what leaves no trace in any data, there is no shortcut: people have to keep looking at the real thing. An empty dashboard is the right goal. But silence is a claim, and like any claim, it has to be earned.
