This is not a criticism. A standard textbook, Mathematics for Machine Learning, covers what an engineer needs in four parts: linear algebra, analytic geometry, calculus and probability, plus some optimization (Deisenroth et al. 2020). None of it would surprise a good student from 1950.

title: The Mathematics Still to Come
text:
The claim
Stated precisely, the claim of this analysis has three parts.

Enough to build. The mathematics used to design and train modern models (Table 1) is almost entirely older than the models.
Not enough to explain. For four phenomena (generalization in models with more parameters than examples, scaling laws, sudden changes in ability, and internal representations), no existing theory predicts from first principles how production-scale models behave: their exponents, constants, thresholds or features.
New concepts will be needed. The theory that does will need new macroscopic concepts, quantities that summarize billions of parameters the way temperature and entropy summarize a gas, and not only new results within existing frameworks.

The first part is a matter of record. The second is my reading of the literature as of November 2026. The third is a hunch, and the last sections say what would prove it wrong.

title: The Mathematics Still to Come
section: What the old mathematics cannot explain
text:
What the old mathematics cannot explain
The old mathematics is enough to build these machines. The trouble begins when we ask it to explain them. Four things stand out.
They generalize when they should not. Classical learning theory warns that a model with far more parameters than training examples can simply memorize its data, and its guarantees then say nothing about new cases. Modern networks have far more parameters than examples, and they generalize anyway. Zhang and colleagues showed that standard networks can perfectly memorize images with random labels, which means they have the capacity to overfit, yet on real labels they generalize well (Zhang et al. 2017). Belkin and colleagues then showed that test error, as models grow, can get worse and then better again, a “double descent” the classical picture did not predict (Belkin et al. 2019; Belkin 2021).



Figure 1. Top: the classical picture. As a model grows, test error first falls, then rises once the model is large enough to memorize its data. Bottom: what is often seen in practice, a peak near that point, then error falls again. The bottom curve describes what happens, not what is worth doing: it says nothing about cost. Illustrative curves in the shape described by Belkin and colleagues, not data.


Their error follows laws we did not derive. When language models are scaled up, their error falls along smooth power laws in the number of parameters, the amount of data and the compute, across several orders of magnitude (Kaplan et al. 2020). These laws are measured, not derived, and they can be revised: two years later, another team found that the best balance between model size and data was quite different, and their correction pointed toward smaller models, not bigger ones. A 70-billion-parameter model trained on more data beat one four times its size (Hoffmann et al. 2022). A law whose constants move when someone measures more carefully is a sign that the theory underneath is missing. A power law also carries a warning that is easy to miss: each equal step down in error costs many times more than the last. The curves describe diminishing returns, not a promise.
Their skills appear suddenly. In some training runs, a network memorizes its training set early, shows no sign of understanding for a long time, and then abruptly generalizes, a behaviour called “grokking” (Power et al. 2022). In one small case the mystery was solved by looking inside: a network learning addition modulo a prime had found, on its own, a method built on Fourier’s sines and cosines (Nanda et al. 2023). For large models the picture is murkier. Abilities that seem to appear suddenly with scale (Wei et al. 2022) can look smooth when they are measured differently (Schaeffer et al. 2023), which is itself a sign that we do not yet know which quantities to measure. We see something like phase transitions in learning; we do not have a good theory of when and why they happen.
We do not know what is inside. Networks seem to store more concepts than they have dimensions, by packing them along nearly perpendicular directions, a phenomenon called superposition (Elhage et al. 2022). Researchers have since pulled millions of such directions, many of them readable as concepts, out of a production language model (Templeton et al. 2024). Small, invisible changes to an input can flip a model’s answer (Szegedy et al. 2014). We can measure all of this. We cannot yet predict it from first principles.

title: The Mathematics Still to Come
text:
The theory so far
To be fair to the field: machine learning has not only borrowed mathematics; it has created some. Vapnik and Chervonenkis built a theory of how a learner generalizes from finite data (Vapnik and Chervonenkis 1971), Leslie Valiant defined what it means to be learnable at all (Valiant 1984), and the needs of data science have reshaped probability in high dimensions (Vershynin 2018). That theory was built for an earlier generation of models, and the puzzles above are the places where it stops predicting what we see.
Newer theory is real too. The neural tangent kernel describes very wide networks (Jacot et al. 2018); mean-field theories describe how small networks learn (Mei et al. 2018); statistical physics has long been applied to learning (Bahri et al. 2020); an effective theory of deep networks is built on the ratio of depth to width (Roberts et al. 2022); and a theory of scaling laws links their exponents to the dimension of the data (Bahri et al. 2024). Theory has also changed practice at least once: a study of infinitely wide networks gave a way to tune training settings on a 40-million-parameter model and carry them over to a 6.7-billion-parameter one, beating published results for that size (Yang and Hu 2021; Yang et al. 2022). In 2026, fourteen researchers argued that these strands are converging into a scientific theory of deep learning, which they propose to call “learning mechanics” (Simon et al. 2026). These are, I think, early signs of a Carnot. But practice is still far ahead of theory, and most theory explains a simplified network rather than the systems we actually use.

title: The Mathematics Still to Come
section: A precedent: the engine before the theory
text:
A precedent: the engine before the theory
Thomas Newcomen’s steam engine was pumping water out of mines from 1712. James Watt’s separate condenser, which made it efficient, dates from 1769 (Hills 1989). Engines powered an industrial revolution, and for all that time nobody could say what an engine fundamentally was, or what limited its efficiency. The answer came in 1824, when Sadi Carnot asked how much work could, in principle, be drawn from heat (Carnot 1824). He reasoned with the caloric theory, which treated heat as a fluid and was wrong. His central result survived anyway, and in the 1850s Clausius and others rebuilt it on firmer ground. Clausius named entropy in 1865 (Clausius 1865). In 1877, Boltzmann explained it as counting: entropy measures how many microscopic arrangements are compatible with what we see at the macroscopic scale (Boltzmann 1877).



Figure 2. Steam engines ran for more than a century before thermodynamics explained them. Learning machines have been built and run since the perceptron; the explanation is still open. Both lanes share the same time scale. Schematic, my own; dates from the references.


Four lessons carry over.

The machine came first. Practice led, and theory followed by more than a century. That is how much of science has worked.
The theory was new. Thermodynamics was not a better engineering manual. It introduced concepts, like entropy and temperature in its modern sense, that turned out to matter far beyond engines.
An early theory does not need to be right to point the way. Carnot’s caloric was wrong; his question was right.
The key move was to stop looking at the parts. Nobody explained the engine by tracking each molecule of steam. When there are enough molecules, a few macroscopic quantities obey exact laws because the details average out. The large number was not the obstacle. It was the solution.

That last lesson matters most for machine learning. We keep trying to understand models with billions of parameters neuron by neuron. Perhaps, like steam, they will be understood instead through laws that only appear at scale. That is not an argument for ever larger machines. Thermodynamics did not make engines bigger; it made them better, by showing where the heat was wasted.
The same pattern runs through the history of mathematics. Fourier invented his series to solve the problem of heat flow (Fourier 1822); Fisher invented much of modern statistics to analyse agricultural experiments (Fisher 1925); Shannon invented information theory for communication engineering (Shannon 1948); physicists used Dirac’s delta function (Dirac 1930) for about two decades before Laurent Schwartz gave it a rigorous home (Schwartz 1950). Sometimes the mathematics is already waiting: Riemann presented his geometry in 1854, sixty years before Einstein needed it for gravity (Riemann 1868; Einstein 1915), an instance of what Wigner called the “unreasonable effectiveness” of mathematics (Wigner 1960). Machine learning will probably see both: mathematics borrowed from shelves where it has been waiting, and mathematics invented because nothing on the shelves fits.

title: The Mathematics Still to Come
text:
Five mathematics we may need
What follows are hunches. Each points to a real gap and has early work around it, but nobody knows yet which, if any, will grow into a field.
A thermodynamics of learning. The scaling laws are to AI what Boyle’s law was to gases (Boyle 1662): an empirical regularity with no derivation behind it. We need the equivalent of kinetic theory: a mathematics that starts from what training does at the microscopic scale and derives the macroscopic laws, with their constants, and says when they will break. That probably means new macroscopic quantities, the equivalents of temperature and entropy for a network in training. Statistical physics has started this work (Bahri et al. 2020; Roberts et al. 2022), the first derivations of scaling laws from properties of the data have appeared (Bahri et al. 2024), and the proposed “learning mechanics” (Simon et al. 2026) is, in effect, a programme for exactly this. The field has a name now, if not yet its Boltzmann.
A geometry of meaning. Inside a network, concepts seem to live as directions in a space of thousands of dimensions, packed more densely than the dimensions should allow (Elhage et al. 2022). In such spaces almost all directions are nearly perpendicular, which is what lets so many concepts coexist. There is evidence that many concepts are represented as straight lines, and a first attempt to say in which geometry “straight” should be measured (Park et al. 2024). “Geometric deep learning” already uses symmetry and group theory to design networks (Bronstein et al. 2021). What we lack is a mathematics of the representations networks learn: how concepts combine, how meaning is composed, which approximate symmetries emerge from data. I suspect it will be a geometry of soft, approximate structure, where the exact objects of classical geometry become statistical ones.
A theory of singularities and sudden change. Classical statistics assumes that each setting of a model’s parameters gives a different behaviour, and that near the best setting the landscape looks like a smooth bowl. Neural networks violate both assumptions. Sumio Watanabe showed that, for such singular models, the right measure of complexity is not the number of parameters but a quantity from algebraic geometry, computed with Hironaka’s resolution of singularities, a deep result from 1964 (Watanabe 2009; Hironaka 1964): a striking case of mathematics waiting on a shelf. Researchers can now estimate a local version of Watanabe’s quantity for real networks, including transformer language models (Lau et al. 2025). My hunch is that this is the beginning of a larger theory that would explain grokking and other sudden jumps in ability as transitions between singular regions, and predict when they happen.
A mathematics of guarantees for things we did not design. Engineering has always relied on proofs about things we designed: this bridge carries that load, this program terminates. A trained network was not designed line by line; it was grown. We want guarantees about it: that it will not do certain things, that its answers lie within a bound, that a small change in input will not flip its decision. Early tools exist: some verify properties of small networks exactly (Katz et al. 2017), others certify that a classifier’s answer cannot be flipped by changes below a given size (Cohen et al. 2019). They do not yet scale to the systems we use, or to the properties we care most about. The mathematics we have for proving properties of programs is not built for objects of this size and kind. It may take a new mixture of logic, probability and geometry: statements true not with certainty but with a quantified confidence, about functions nobody wrote.
A dynamics of machines in a loop. Models are increasingly trained on text that earlier models wrote, and they act in a world their outputs have already changed. Recursive training on generated data can make models lose the rare parts of the original distribution, a failure called model collapse (Shumailov et al. 2024); in some settings, keeping the real data and adding generated data to it avoids the collapse (Gerstgrasser et al. 2024). The answer depends on the structure of the loop, and we have no general theory of that structure. Learners that learn from each other, and from people who learn from them, form a dynamical system closer to ecology or economics than to the fixed datasets of classical theory. Its mathematics barely exists.



Figure 3. The five hunches as a map: each puzzle we observe, the mathematics it may call for, and the early work around it. Only the hunches are mine; the early work is cited in the text. Schematic, my own.


The five have something in common. None is about a single small network. All are about large, typical behaviour: very many parameters, very many examples, very many interacting systems. The mathematics we lack is, I suspect, the mathematics of the many.

title: The Mathematics Still to Come
text:
Two objections
We may not need theory at all. Richard Sutton’s “bitter lesson” is that, over seventy years, general methods that use more computation have beaten methods built on human insight (Sutton 2019). Engineering got here without theory; why should it need theory now? I think the lesson has been right about the past and is a weaker guide to the future. Scale costs energy and money, and the supply of human-written text is finite: one study estimates that, if current trends continue, the largest training runs will use up the stock of public human text sometime between 2026 and 2032 (Villalobos et al. 2024). The bitter lesson also says nothing against understanding why scale works. Steam engines improved for decades by trial and error; thermodynamics then told engineers where the limits were and what to stop trying. We will need the same: to know what a system cannot do, how far a trend can go, and what might happen inside it that we would not like. And, as I argued in Not Because It Is Useful, wanting to understand is not only a means to better machines. It is a reason in itself.
AI will invent this mathematics for us. In 2026, this stopped being a thought experiment. After competition milestones (olympiad silver in 2024 and gold in 2025 (AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry teams 2024; Hubert et al. 2025; Google DeepMind 2025)) and early help with research (Romera-Paredes et al. 2024; Davies et al. 2021), machines reached research problems themselves. In May 2026, a general-purpose reasoning model from OpenAI disproved a conjecture Erdős made in 1946 about how many pairs of points in the plane can lie at the same distance; according to the company, external mathematicians checked the proof (OpenAI 2026). On 6 October, the company released more than 700 research papers produced with its models (Calegari 2026), among them a proof of the “quasi-Riemann hypothesis”, a weaker cousin of the Riemann hypothesis, which, Quanta reports, experts have studied and take seriously (Quanta Magazine 2026). A claimed solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem, announced in September, is disputed and, according to MIT Technology Review, has not been accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute (MIT Technology Review 2026). Even setting that one aside, machines are now partners in mathematical research. On 1 November, in a guest post on Terence Tao’s blog, the mathematician Frank Calegari called that release “a watershed in the history of mathematics” and wrote that AI “is now undeniably capable of making groundbreaking contributions across many areas of mathematics”. He was just as blunt about its limits: “despite some tremendous ideas”, the papers “are atrociously written and violate our community expectations of attribution. Some of them are even wrong” (Calegari 2026).
But the hardest step in the stories above was never the proof. It was the concept: Carnot’s ideal engine, Boltzmann’s entropy as counting, Shannon’s decision to measure information without caring about meaning. Each was a choice of what to look at, made because it made a whole field understandable. Here the quasi-Riemann proof is revealing. According to the experts Quanta spoke to, it introduced no new concepts: it found unexpected connections between existing ones (Quanta Magazine 2026). That is an extraordinary achievement, and the line between connecting old concepts and inventing new ones is thinner than my argument would like. Boltzmann’s entropy was, in a sense, a new connection between mechanics and probability. So I hold this part loosely: machines may cross that line soon. Calegari makes a related point from inside mathematics: even if the release had solved every problem in the Langlands programme, thinking it had “solved number theory” “would be as naive as saying that the construction of the periodic table solved chemistry”. Solving a central problem “is not the end but the first step to finding new playgrounds to explore” (Calegari 2026). And if proofs become abundant, the scarce work becomes checking them and understanding them. The test of the new mathematics will still be whether we understand more because of it.

title: The Mathematics Still to Come
text:
What I am not claiming

That there is no theory. There is a great deal, some of it guiding practice. My claim is that it does not yet explain the systems we actually use.
That bigger is the future. Double descent and scaling laws describe what happens, not what is worth doing. A theory of scale should tell us when to stop scaling.
That the five hunches are the right list. They are guesses about the shape of what is missing. The new mathematics could come from somewhere none of them points to.
That machines cannot invent concepts. The 2026 results suggest they may, soon. I am claiming only that, so far, the reported breakthroughs connect existing concepts rather than introduce new ones.
That the Carnot is far away. It may be arriving now, with “learning mechanics” or something else. The claim is about the shape of the missing theory, not its date.
That the 2026 results are settled. Some come from company announcements and press coverage; the Navier–Stokes claim in particular is disputed, and even an enthusiastic reader of the October release notes that some of its papers are wrong (Calegari 2026).

title: The Mathematics Still to Come
text:
What would prove me wrong

Old mathematics turns out to be enough (part 3 of the claim). If, by 2030, a theory derives the exponents and constants of scaling laws for real transformer training using only existing tools, with no new concepts, the claim that new mathematics is needed is wrong.
The parts are enough. If interpretability explains large models neuron by neuron, with no need for macroscopic quantities, the “mathematics of the many” is wrong.
There are no real transitions. If every sudden jump in ability turns out to be an artefact of measurement, the hunch about singularities and sudden change loses its main motivation.
Theory never reaches the design table. If, by 2030, the leading labs still choose model size, data and training budget only from fitted curves and trial runs, with no derived theory telling them where the limits are, the bitter lesson wins this round, and my case for theory as a practical need is wrong.
The hunches stay empty. If, by 2030, none of the five has produced a result that predicts something about production-scale models before it is measured, they were the wrong list.
A machine introduces a concept mathematicians adopt. If an AI system proposes a new definition or structure that becomes a field of its own, the line I draw between proofs and concepts falls.

title: The Mathematics Still to Come
text:
What follows for practitioners
If you work with machine learning and have no plans to invent mathematics, five things follow, I think.

Learn the old mathematics well. Linear algebra, probability and calculus are the language in which everything else, including the new mathematics, will be written.
Watch where it breaks. When a model generalizes better than it should, fails suddenly, or a curve bends where no theory said it would, you are at the edge of the map. Write those surprises down.
Do not assume bigger is better. Giving a model more time to reason when it answers can, on some problems, let a small model outperform one fourteen times larger (Snell et al. 2025). The useful question is when a large model is needed and when a small, fast one will do, a theme I took up in Fast AI.
Check before you trust, and understand before you build on it. Calegari’s verdict on the October papers, “tremendous ideas” but some “even wrong” (Calegari 2026), is a reminder that when results become cheap to produce, the scarce work is verifying and understanding them. The same holds for a model’s outputs, and for claims about models.
Keep some humility about explanations. Many of the stories we tell about why models work are, today, stories. We are in the position of engineers in 1800: excellent at building engines, and honest enough to admit that we do not yet know what they are.

The steam engine ran for a century before someone asked the right question about it, and the answer reached far beyond engines. The machines we have built are, among other things, a question addressed to mathematics. The strange twist of 2026 is that the machines have started to help answer it. Whether we understand the answer will still be up to us.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
text:
Overview, November 2026. A map of the research from 2020 to 2026 on one question: can a neural network learn well with only local rules, and can it build the machinery that does the learning, instead of having it designed? It starts from a paper published in PNAS in October 2026 (Liao et al. 2026) and places it among about twenty openly accessible sources, mostly from 2020 to 2026, with two earlier papers as background. I chose works that are cited often, are open access or have a free preprint, and stand for a distinct line of work; the list is not complete. I read them through their abstracts, their preprints and the publishers’ or institutes’ summaries, not always in full, so I keep to what those state and give numbers only where a source gives them. The five figures are schematics of my own, drawn with figs.py; they simplify the ideas and show no data.
In short. In a standard neural network, people design everything that makes learning happen: the wiring, the rule that changes each connection, and the backward pass that tells each connection how to change. The brain has no such designer, which is why neuroscientists have long doubted that it runs backpropagation. Work since 2020 has relaxed the design step by step. A first line keeps the rules local but lets feedback connections learn or settle until they carry useful error signals, and gets close to backpropagation on real benchmarks. A second line drops the backward pass altogether. A third uses an outer loop to learn the plasticity rule itself. A fourth, the newest, lets structure emerge: networks that grow their own wiring, and, in the PNAS paper, circuits that assemble out of random connections under simple local rules and then behave like gradient descent. My reading: the result is real and interesting, but it moves the design rather than removing it. Someone still chooses the local rules; what emerges is the circuit that turns them into learning. That is already a lot. It suggests that learning may be less an algorithm we must install than a property that well-chosen local dynamics fall into.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
text:
1. The question
A deep network learns by changing millions of connection strengths a little at a time. To know which way to change one connection, it needs to know how that connection affected the error at the output, many layers away. Backpropagation computes this exactly: it sends the error backwards through the network, using the same weights as the forward pass, transposed. This is the credit assignment problem, and backpropagation is the reference answer.
For a brain, the answer looks wrong in at least three ways. A synapse would need to know the strength of a different synapse, on the backward path, and keep it exactly equal to its own: the weight transport problem. The backward pass would need a separate, precisely timed phase. And the derivatives it carries are not obviously something a neuron computes. For decades this was taken as a sign that the brain does something else.



Figure 1. The weight transport problem. In backpropagation, the error travels back through a copy of the forward weights, transposed, so each synapse would need to know the strength of another. Feedback alignment uses fixed random feedback instead; learned feedback lets the feedback weights adjust themselves from local activity. Schematic, my own.


In 2020, Lillicrap, Santoro, Marris, Akerman and Hinton reopened the question in a review that framed this period of research (Lillicrap et al. 2020). Their argument was that the brain could use feedback connections to induce neural activity whose local differences encode error signals close to those of backpropagation. The brain would not run backpropagation; it would approximate its effect with signals each synapse can see.
The question this overview follows goes one step further. Even if local signals can approximate the gradient, someone still has to design the circuit that produces them. Who does that in a brain? There is no engineer. So the deeper question is whether the learning machinery itself can come from local interactions: grow, assemble, or be found by a slower process such as evolution.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
text:
2. A map
Figure 2 sorts the work by one question: what does the designer still fix? I separate three things a designer can fix: the wiring (which neurons connect), the plasticity rule (how a connection changes, given what it can see), and the learning circuit (whatever produces the error signals that tell connections how to change: in backpropagation, the exact backward pass).



Figure 2. Five lines of work on learning with local rules, 2020 to 2026, sorted by what the designer still fixes: the wiring, the plasticity rule, and the learning circuit that carries error signals. Moving down, more is learned or emerges. Two placements are simplifications: in the learned-rules row, the circuit in which the rule acts is usually designed, though Lindsey and Litwin-Kumar also meta-learn the feedback; in the last row, neural cellular automata grow shapes, not learning machinery, and are there as the origin of the growth idea. In that row, the wiring emerges in growing networks and the learning circuit emerges in self-assembling learning; the local rules remain designed. Placement is my own reading of the cited work. Schematic, my own.


Table 1 gives the same works with what each one claims, in the authors’ terms.
Table 1. Representative work, 2019 to 2026. Results are as reported by the authors; they come from different tasks and settings and should not be compared across rows.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
text:
3. Approximating backpropagation with local signals
The largest body of work keeps the goal of backpropagation, a gradient, and asks how to get it with signals a synapse can see. Figure 3 shows three of the ideas side by side.



Figure 3. Three ways to carry an error signal with local information. In equilibrium propagation, each synapse compares its activity in a free and a nudged state. In predictive coding, error units compute the difference between activity and prediction, and each weight changes with that error and its own input. In burst-dependent plasticity, a burst strengthens a recently active synapse and a single spike weakens it, so feedback that changes the burst rate acts as a teaching signal. Simplified from the cited papers. Schematic, my own.


Learning the feedback. The simplest trick, feedback alignment (Figure 1, middle), sends errors back through fixed random weights; the forward weights then come to align with them. It works for shallow networks and struggles on hard tasks. Just before this period, Akrout and colleagues showed two ways for the feedback path to learn good weights without copying them: a “weight mirror” circuit, and a variant of an old algorithm by Kolen and Pollack. On ImageNet both outperformed feedback alignment and nearly matched backpropagation (Akrout et al. 2019). This is the first hint of the theme of this overview: part of the learning machinery need not be designed if it can learn itself.
Letting the network settle. Predictive coding treats each layer as predicting the one below and passes prediction errors around. Millidge, Tschantz and Buckley showed that, with only local and mostly Hebbian updates, it converges to the exact backpropagation gradients, not only in layered networks but on arbitrary computation graphs, including CNNs, RNNs and LSTMs, and performs on par with backpropagation on their benchmarks (Millidge et al. 2020). The exact match needs a simplification, the fixed prediction assumption, which holds each layer’s prediction fixed while errors settle; Rosenbaum showed that, under it, predictive coding performs the same computation as backpropagation, and reviews of the field have questioned how a brain would implement it (Rosenbaum 2022; Millidge et al. 2021). Equilibrium propagation follows a related idea: let the network settle, nudge the output toward the target, let it settle again, and update each connection from the difference between the two states. It had struggled to scale; Laborieux and colleagues traced the problem to a bias in the gradient estimate, removed most of it with nudges in both directions, and reached 11.7% test error on CIFAR-10 with a deep convolutional network, close to backpropagation through time. The method in its original form assumes symmetric connections, the same weight in both directions, which is the weight transport problem again; a variant with separate forward and backward connections reached 13.2% (Laborieux et al. 2021).
Using what neurons actually do. Payeur and colleagues started from the biology. If plasticity depends on high-frequency bursts of spikes, so that a burst strengthens a synapse and a single spike weakens it, then neurons higher in a hierarchy can coordinate the learning of lower ones; it works, they report, together with short-term synaptic dynamics, active apical dendrites and plasticity in the feedback pathways (Payeur et al. 2021). For recurrent spiking networks, Bellec and colleagues proposed e-prop: each synapse keeps a local eligibility trace and combines it with a learning signal sent from above, which avoids storing and replaying the network’s history. It approaches the performance of backpropagation through time and suits low-power neuromorphic chips (Bellec et al. 2020).
Changing the order. Song, Bogacz and colleagues went beyond approximation. In prospective configuration, the network first infers the activity it should have after learning, and only then changes the weights to consolidate it; backpropagation does the reverse. They report that this learns more efficiently than backpropagation in situations animals face, such as deep structures and online learning, and explains behavioural and neural data that backpropagation does not (Song et al. 2024). This is the first sign that the brain’s way might be better for its job, not a weaker copy.
What this line shows: the gradient does not need a designed backward pass, as long as feedback connections are present and their dynamics are right. What it still assumes: someone designed those dynamics.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
text:
4. Learning without a backward pass
A smaller line asks whether the gradient is needed at all.
Hinton’s Forward-Forward algorithm replaces the forward and backward passes with two forward passes, one on real data and one on “negative” data, and gives each layer its own objective: high “goodness” for real data, low for negative (Hinton 2022). Hinton presented it as preliminary, shown to work on a few small problems; one practical promise is that the negative passes could be done offline, so that learning on the real data needs no stored activities.
SoftHebb goes further: no feedback, no target, no error signal of any kind, only Hebbian learning in soft winner-take-all layers, with a linear classifier on top. With up to five hidden layers, Journé and colleagues report 99.4% on MNIST, 80.3% on CIFAR-10, 76.2% on STL-10 and 27.3% on ImageNet (Journé et al. 2023). Those numbers are far from the state of the art on hard tasks, but they are the best I found for learning that is purely local in this strong sense.
What this line shows: a lot can be learned with no credit assignment across layers. What it does not show yet: that this is enough for hard problems.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
text:
5. Learning the learning rule
The third line stops designing the plasticity rule and lets an outer loop find it, often by evolution or gradient descent over the rule’s few parameters. The network still learns with local rules during its “lifetime”; the rule itself is the product of a slower process, as it would be in biology (Figure 4).



Figure 4. Learning the learning rule. In the fast loop, a network starts from random weights and a local rule with parameters θ changes them while it lives through its task. In the slow loop, evolution or meta-learning scores how well each lifetime went and adjusts θ. Schematic, my own.


Confavreux, Zenke, Agnes, Lillicrap and Vogels framed it clearly: judge a plasticity rule not by how well it fits recordings, but by what function it carves into a random network. Their search rediscovered Oja’s rule, a classic rule that extracts the main direction of variation in the input, and, at network level, Oja’s rule paired with an anti-Hebbian rule that extracts several components; they also found rules for spiking networks with plastic inhibition (Confavreux et al. 2020). Jordan, Schmidt, Senn and Petrovici evolved rules as compact symbolic expressions, so that people can read them, and report new mechanisms for learning from reward, gradient-descent-like rules for learning from targets, and STDP-like rules with homeostasis (Jordan et al. 2021).
Najarro and Risi went to the extreme: start from completely random weights and evolve only the synapse-specific Hebbian rules. The rules alone let a simulated robot learn to walk, and adapt to damage it had not seen in training, with no reward signal during its lifetime (Najarro and Risi 2020). Reviewers at NeurIPS noted that fixed, trained weights still did better in some settings (reviews).
Two studies brought feedback back in. Lindsey and Litwin-Kumar meta-learned networks that use feedback connections and local plasticity, with feedback not tied to the forward weights; they matched or exceeded a gradient-based online meta-learning method and did particularly well at continual learning (Lindsey and Litwin-Kumar 2020). Shervani-Tabar and Rosenbaum meta-learned one shared, interpretable rule on top of random feedback, and report improved online learning in deep networks with little data, a setting where feedback alignment learns slowly (Shervani-Tabar and Rosenbaum 2023).
Kirsch and Schmidhuber asked the broadest version: if every weight is replaced by a tiny shared recurrent network, can the whole system learn how to learn? They show that weight sharing and sparsity are enough to express powerful learning algorithms; that such a system can implement backpropagation in its forward dynamics alone; and that it can meta-learn new algorithms that, in their tests, improve on backpropagation and generalise to new datasets (Kirsch and Schmidhuber 2021).
What this line shows: plasticity rules are not sacred; they can be found, and sometimes found rules beat designed ones. What it still assumes: a designed outer loop, and usually a designed circuit in which the rule acts.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
text:
6. Growing the machinery
The newest line lets structure itself emerge.
Growing wiring. In 2020, Mordvintsev, Randazzo, Niklasson and Levin trained neural cellular automata: a grid of cells, each running the same small network and talking only to its neighbours, that grows a target image from a single cell and regrows it after damage (Mordvintsev et al. 2020). It was about shapes, not learning, but it showed that robust global structure can come from purely local rules. Najarro, Sudhakaran and Risi applied the idea to networks themselves: a neural developmental program, using only local communication between neurons, grows a network instead of having it designed, and they tested the grown networks on reinforcement and supervised learning (Najarro et al. 2023).
Assembling the learning circuit. The PNAS paper by Liao, Ziyin, Gan and colleagues at MIT takes the last step on my map (Liao et al. 2026). They call the framework Self-Assembling Learning, and its main example a Self-Assembling Motif. According to the abstract, the motif can emerge from random connectivity under heterosynaptic plasticity (in general, rules in which a synapse changes with the activity of other synapses on the same neuron, not only its own), and, repeated across layers, the motifs self-organise into networks whose dynamics approximate a generalised form of stochastic gradient descent. MIT’s news piece reports image classification comparable to networks trained with backpropagation, and is careful about the biology: whether the brain uses these motifs is not settled (McGovern Institute for Brain Research 2026). I could read only the abstract and that summary, not the full paper, so I leave the exact circuit, the conditions and the benchmark numbers to the paper itself. Figure 5 sketches the idea at that level of detail.



Figure 5. The idea of self-assembling learning, simplified. A network starts with random connections; synapses follow a local heterosynaptic rule; a motif with a forward and a feedback stream assembles; stacked motifs make a network whose learning approximates a generalised stochastic gradient descent. This is a sketch of the idea as the authors describe it in their abstract, not the exact circuit of Liao and colleagues’ paper. Schematic, my own.


A 2025 preprint by Ziyin, Chuang and Poggio, Heterosynaptic Circuits Are Universal Gradient Machines, generalises the idea and, in the authors’ words, proposes “a design principle for the learning circuits of the biological brain” (Ziyin et al. 2025).
What is new here, compared with the earlier lines, is where the design stops. In Section 3, someone designed the feedback circuit. In Section 5, an outer loop found the rule, but within a designed circuit. Here, the rules are fixed and simple, and the circuit that makes them add up to gradient learning is not designed at all: it falls out of the dynamics.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
section: 7. What is established, what is open
text:
7. What is established, what is open
Established, in the sense that several groups report it:

Local signals can approximate backpropagation’s gradients closely, in theory and on benchmarks up to ImageNet, provided feedback connections exist (Akrout et al. 2019; Millidge et al. 2020; Laborieux et al. 2021).
Weight transport is not required: feedback can learn its own weights, or be random, if the forward weights or the rule adapt (Akrout et al. 2019; Shervani-Tabar and Rosenbaum 2023).
Plasticity rules can be discovered by an outer loop, and found rules can rediscover classic ones or do better than hand-designed ones in narrow tests (Confavreux et al. 2020; Jordan et al. 2021; Kirsch and Schmidhuber 2021).
At least one circuit that implements gradient-like learning can assemble itself from random connectivity under local rules (Liao et al. 2026).

Open:

Scale. Most results are on MNIST, CIFAR-10, small control tasks or, at best, ImageNet. None of these methods has trained anything like a modern language model.
Cost. Settling dynamics, two-phase learning and outer loops cost time. Whether local learning is cheaper in practice depends on hardware; on GPUs, backpropagation is very hard to beat. On neuromorphic chips the answer may differ (Bellec et al. 2020).
Biology. Showing that a mechanism is sufficient does not show that the brain uses it. The burst, heterosynaptic and predictive-coding proposals each make testable predictions; the experiments are hard and mostly not done.
What is still designed. Every system on the map has a designer somewhere: the local rules, the outer loop, or the growth program. Moving the design one level up is progress; it is not the absence of design.

Not covered here. This map leaves out several lines that a specialist would expect: dendritic and multi-compartment neuron models, in which a neuron’s apical dendrite carries the error; target propagation; three-factor rules, in which a neuromodulator such as dopamine gates a local change; and the evidence that biologically motivated methods struggle at scale, which a 2018 study found for target propagation and feedback alignment on ImageNet (Bartunov et al. 2018). Each would deserve its own overview.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
text:
8. My reading
I find the self-assembly result the most interesting on the map, for a reason that is easy to overstate, so let me be precise about it.
It does not show that a network can invent learning from nothing. Someone chose the heterosynaptic rules, and someone chose to stack the motifs in layers. What it shows is that, given those simple local rules, a working learning circuit is something the dynamics fall into, rather than something that must be wired by hand. That changes how I think about backpropagation. It stops looking like an algorithm that a brain would have to implement against all odds, and starts looking like a kind of attractor: a behaviour that many local dynamical systems approach, the way many physical systems settle into the same few patterns. That is a hypothesis, not a result: one paper shows one such system, and I know of no study yet of how general the effect is.
If that is right, two consequences follow. The first is for neuroscience: the search should be for local rules and conditions under which gradient-like learning emerges, not for a hidden backward pass. Several lines here, from bursts to prospective configuration, already point that way. The second is for machine learning, and it is more speculative. Today we fix the architecture and the learning algorithm, then optimise the weights. The lines in Sections 5 and 6 suggest a different split: fix a small set of local rules, and let the structure and part of the learning machinery organise themselves, as the brain must have done. Whether that can ever compete with backpropagation on a GPU, I doubt; whether it matters for systems that must keep learning on their own, with little power and no data centre, I think it might. For now it is a direction, with small-scale evidence, not a replacement.

title: Who Writes the Learning Rule?
text:
9. Where to start

Lillicrap and colleagues, “Backpropagation and the brain” (Lillicrap et al. 2020). The framing for everything since 2020; short, clear and widely cited.
Millidge, Tschantz and Buckley on predictive coding (Millidge et al. 2020). The cleanest result that local rules can give exact gradients.
Confavreux and colleagues on meta-learned plasticity (Confavreux et al. 2020). The idea that rules should be judged by what they build.
Mordvintsev and colleagues, “Growing Neural Cellular Automata” (Mordvintsev et al. 2020). Interactive, open, and the best intuition for structure from local rules.
Liao, Ziyin, Gan and colleagues in PNAS (Liao et al. 2026), with its free preprint. Where the map currently ends.


Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.
Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.


Read next · The Mathematics Still to Come AI runs on old mathematics and works before we understand it. What may have to be invented.


This overview is not exhaustive. It maps representative, openly accessible work from 2020 to 2026 as I could read it, often through abstracts and summaries, and the field moves fast. Missing work and corrections are welcome.
The views in this overview are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

title: A Finite State of Mind
text:
Analysis, November 2026. Three posts I saved this week, read together: a technology executive’s summary of NVIDIA’s paper You don’t need long context (A technology executive 2026; Belcak et al. 2026), Johannes Hermle’s announcement of Anthropic’s report on how researchers use Claude (Hermle 2026; Hermle et al. 2026), and Ramakrushna Mohapatra’s explainer on multi-head, multi-query and grouped-query attention (Mohapatra 2026). I read the paper and the report in full. Every number taken from a source is cited where it is used. The figures are drawn with figs.py: Figure 1 is computed, Figures 2 and 3 plot the sources’ numbers, Figure 4 is my own schematic.
In short. The three posts are about one thing: what a system must hold in mind while it works, and what that costs. Grouped-query attention shrinks the memory per remembered token (Ainslie et al. 2023). The NVIDIA paper shrinks the number of tokens kept: strong models lose little when their history is replaced by a short written state (Belcak et al. 2026, secs. 3–5). The Anthropic report shows that AI is used where research tasks are formal and checkable, and least at the bench (Hermle et al. 2026). The first two levers multiply, and all three meet in one place: the best compaction NVIDIA found has the shape of a lab notebook. What does not fit on the page, the sample, the instrument, the question worth asking, is where the bottleneck and the human part of the work remain.

title: A Finite State of Mind
text:
Three posts, one resource
The executive’s post: late tokens cost up to 7 times more than early ones, aggressive compaction costs little accuracy, and “your agent doesn’t need a photographic memory. It needs a good notepad. It’s Guy Pearce in Memento and it still ships the PR” (A technology executive 2026). Hermle’s post: Claude is used most per researcher in computer science, mathematics and statistics, use tracks AI capability, and output could double in some fields, with physical work as the bottleneck (Hermle 2026). Mohapatra’s post: decoding is limited by memory, because every generated token reads the whole key-value (KV) cache; for a Llama 3 8B-shaped model, multi-head attention (MHA) stores 512 KiB per token, multi-query attention (MQA) 16 KiB, and grouped-query attention (GQA) sits between (Mohapatra 2026).
What ties them is the working state: what a system keeps at hand to take its next step. For a transformer it is the KV cache (Pope et al. 2023):

\text{KV bytes} = B \times N, \qquad B = 2\,L\,H_{kv}\,d\,b,

where B, the bytes per token, is set by the architecture (L layers, H_{kv} key-value heads of dimension d, b bytes per number), and N, the tokens kept, is set by the harness that runs the model. The attention post is about B. The NVIDIA paper is about N. The Anthropic report is about what comes before both: which work can be turned into tokens at all.

title: A Finite State of Mind
section: The first lever: bytes per token
text:
The first lever: bytes per token
The attention post’s numbers check out: 2 \times 32 \times 32 \times 128 \times 2 bytes is 512 KiB per token with 32 K/V heads, 128 KiB with the 8 that Llama 3 uses (Llama Team 2024), 16 KiB with one (my arithmetic, in figs.py). GQA, introduced in 2023, keeps most of MHA’s quality at most of MQA’s speed (Ainslie et al. 2023). Since then the lever has been pulled hard: DeepSeek’s latent attention caches about 69 KiB per token for a 671-billion-parameter model (my arithmetic from its published configuration (DeepSeek-AI 2024a, 2024b)), sliding windows and token eviction keep fewer tokens per layer (Xiao et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2023), and state space models carry a fixed-size state (Gu and Dao 2023), which hybrids such as Nemotron-H use in place of most attention layers (NVIDIA 2025). Yet N kept growing: several context windows now exceed War and Peace (Belcak et al. 2026, table 1).

title: A Finite State of Mind
text:
The second lever: tokens kept
The NVIDIA paper asks whether long contexts are necessary, and answers no (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 1 and 6).
The cost. On H100 GPUs under load, serving a 256K window instead of 16K costs 3.6 times more per generated token for GLM 5.2, 5.6 for Kimi K2.6 and 7 for Qwen 3 Coder Next (Belcak et al. 2026, fig. 1 and 4). So the post’s “up to 7x” is right, with a nuance: it is about the window a server reserves, not the position of one token.
The method. A minimal agent, one Bash command per turn, runs in three regimes: full history; compaction when the context crosses a threshold, after which a fresh conversation starts from the task and a written recap; and compaction after every single action (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 2.4). Long documents stay on disk and are read with grep and bounded reads.
The results. Across six long-horizon benchmarks, compaction moves accuracy between −3.7 and +5.6 points for Claude Opus 4.5 and between −3.3 and +4.4 for GPT 5.6 Sol (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 3). On long-input tasks, selective reading usually beats pasting everything in: RULER recall rises from 62.5% to 95.7% for Opus (Belcak et al. 2026, table 15). Figure 2 shows the most striking result.



Figure 2. One action per context against full history and the best compaction, on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.1. Top: accuracy. Bottom: the largest single context per task; full history reaches 130K to 200K tokens, one action per context a median of 7K to 9K. Data from Table 2 of the paper (Belcak et al. 2026); chart my own.


From this the authors propose a semantic state space model: a model trained to read a written state, take one action, and rewrite the state so that another instance can continue. Unlike Mamba’s hidden state, this one is “explainable natural language” (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 5.1).
Three caveats. The savings assume prices that follow serving cost; at today’s flat prices, compaction sometimes costs more, as for GPT 5.6 Sol on SWE-bench Verified (Belcak et al. 2026, table 3). The result holds for strong models: one open model collapsed from 53.0% to 3.6% under tight compaction (Belcak et al. 2026, app. D, table 9). And the benchmarks have checkable ends; the authors themselves show that a task needing the i-th of many coin tosses must eventually fail under any fixed budget (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 3.1).

title: A Finite State of Mind
text:
The levers multiply
Because the two levers act on different factors, their effects multiply (Figure 1).



Figure 1. KV cache of one sequence for a Llama 3 8B-shaped model in FP16, by tokens kept (rows) and attention layout (columns), and how many sequences fit in 64 GiB, roughly what an 80 GB GPU has left after the weights. 32K is the median largest context of full-history agents in the paper, 8K the median with one action per context (Belcak et al. 2026, table 2). Computed in figs.py; my own.


From MHA at 256K (128 GiB, which does not fit) to GQA at 8K (1 GiB, 64 sequences at once), the cache shrinks 128 times: 4 from the architecture, 32 from the harness. That compares the window a server must reserve. For a typical task the factor is smaller: full-history agents peak at a median of 32K tokens (Belcak et al. 2026, table 2), so going to 8K saves 4 times, and GQA another 4, about 16 times in all. Either way the harness lever matches or beats the architecture, needs no retraining, and anyone who writes an agent can pull it today.

title: A Finite State of Mind
section: The third lever: what can be written down
text:
The third lever: what can be written down
The report never mentions context or tokens. Reading its findings as a statement about what can be written down is my interpretation, and I flag it as such.
The Anthropic report classifies 207,049 research sessions from August and September 2026 by field and task, and adds a survey of 528 scientists (Hermle et al. 2026). Computer science is 4.3% of the world’s researchers but 32.7% of Claude Code sessions; data analysis is the largest task, ideation one of the smallest, although scientists rate it the most important (Hermle et al. 2026). Use rises with how well AI could do a task, and that capability correlates with how well the task suits reinforcement learning (+0.78), that is, with having a checkable result; it falls with the physical share of the task (−0.57) (Hermle et al. 2026).
A simple production model, where the slowest step limits the rest, turns this into scenarios (Figure 3). With today’s abilities widely adopted, output rises up to about 2x in statistics and computer science. If AI did every non-physical step, low-physical fields would reach 15 to 16 times, but bench sciences only 3 to 4, because physical steps take about 40% of their research time, against 4% in the median field (Hermle et al. 2026). The authors call these “illustrative scenarios, not forecasts” (Hermle et al. 2026).



Figure 3. Research output for a fixed budget, relative to no AI, in two scenarios of the Anthropic report. Top: today’s abilities, widely adopted. Bottom: all non-physical steps done by AI; the darker bar is the low end of the stated range. Data from the report (Hermle et al. 2026); chart my own.


The worry behind it is old. Ideas are getting harder to find (Bloom et al. 2020), partly because each researcher must absorb more before contributing: the “burden of knowledge” (Jones 2009). Seen from the first two posts, that is science’s long-context problem.

title: A Finite State of Mind
text:
Where the three meet
The NVIDIA team found that the best compactions are not faithful summaries but “carefully cherry-picked briefs for further execution” (Belcak et al. 2026, app. A). Their recap asks for the objective, established facts kept apart from unverified ideas, changes made, checks run, dead ends, and the next step with “the condition for completion” (Belcak et al. 2026, app. G.1). That is a lab notebook (Figure 4).



Figure 4. The compaction recap used by Belcak et al. (Appendix G.1), item by item, next to the parts of a lab notebook or a scientific paper. Schematic, my own.


Science solved its long-context problem this way, at least since its first journals in 1665. No scientist holds the whole literature in mind. Each reads a compacted state (a review, a textbook), takes a few actions in a career, and writes back an updated state for someone else. Standing on the shoulders of giants is compaction across generations. Read together, the three sources say:

What is checkable may compact well. This is my hypothesis, not a finding of either source. AI is used where results can be checked (Hermle et al. 2026), and a written state works where the task has a verifiable end (Belcak et al. 2026).
The world does not compact. An experiment is the coin-toss case: observations with no structure until you have them. A cell culture’s state is in no context window, which is why about 40% of bench research time resists AI (Hermle et al. 2026). Polanyi said we know more than we can tell (Polanyi 1966); in the lab, much of it is in the hands.
Read selectively. Data analysis is half of Claude Code’s science sessions (Hermle et al. 2026), and agents analyse best by querying, not by pasting (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 4). “A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention” (Simon 1971).

title: A Finite State of Mind
section: What it means for the next few years
text:
What it means for the next few years
Prices that depend on context. If a 256K window costs 3.6 to 7 times more to serve (Belcak et al. 2026, fig. 1), flat prices subsidise long contexts. Expect context tiers, and short-context agents as the default.
Models trained to hand over. The authors expect semantic state models to be “considerably more data-efficient to train” (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 5.1). Writing a good handoff, the skill the collapsing open model lacked, becomes a trained ability.
Agents you can own. At 8K tokens, a GQA model of Llama 3 8B’s shape needs a 1 GiB cache (Figure 1), and the paper runs models locally because data “must remain on-device for privacy or cost reasons” (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 2.3). The executive’s claim that cloud AI is aligned with its owner (A technology executive 2026) is an opinion the paper does not test. What it does show is that a short written state is portable: you can read it, audit it and hand it to another model. You may not own the model; you can own the notepad. That is the shared memory Fast AI needs.
The bottleneck moves to the bench and to the question. Lab automation turns physical steps into tool calls (Boiko et al. 2023), and what remains is ideation, about 4% of sessions today (Hermle et al. 2026).
A state that can be audited, and attacked. A written state can be read by a person, which a neural state never allowed. But whatever enters the notes is believed by every later instance. Keep provenance: where each fact came from, so it can be checked again, as I argued in The Context Is the Wire.

title: A Finite State of Mind
text:
A philosophical perspective
The paper ends by recalling that computability itself assumes “a bounded amount of input at a time and maintaining only a finite state of mind” (Belcak et al. 2026, sec. 6). That is Turing’s 1936 human computer, who sees a few symbols at a time and, when interrupted, leaves a note saying how to continue (Turing 1937). The single-action agent is Turing’s computer, rediscovered at the cost of billions of parameters.
Remembering everything was never the goal. Borges’s Funes remembers every leaf he has seen and cannot think: “To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions” (Borges 1962). Nietzsche held that action needs forgetting (Nietzsche 1874). Full history is Funes; compaction is the forgetting that makes the next step possible.
Memento adds the warning. Leonard lives by notes (Nolan 2000); Clark and Chalmers would say such notes are part of the mind, like Otto’s notebook (Clark and Chalmers 1998). But some of Leonard’s notes are written to deceive him, and Plato’s Thamus warned that writing gives a reminder, not memory, and the look of wisdom without the substance (Plato c. 370 BCE). A mind made of notes is as trustworthy as its notes. That is why the best compaction records how each fact was checked.
And this is what stays ours. A compaction keeps what is relevant to the work ahead, and relevance depends on the aim. The model can write the brief once it has the objective; it cannot tell which objective is worth pursuing. Scientists use AI least for ideation and value it most (Hermle et al. 2026). What remains human is the line at the top of the notebook: the aim, and what is worth remembering for. I argued the same in Not Because It Is Useful.
So keep the notebook short, checked and yours. You may not own the model; you can own the notepad.

title: A Finite State of Mind
text:
Limits

Three kinds of evidence. The cache arithmetic is exact; the NVIDIA costs estimate a price that does not yet exist; the Anthropic data are model-classified sessions from a company that sells the model, and its acceleration figures are scenarios.
Analogies are analogies. A paper is not a compaction prompt, and GQA groups are not research teams.
Short tasks. Most SWE-bench Verified tasks were estimated at under an hour of human work (Chowdhury et al. 2024). Research carries state for months.
My hypothesis. That checkable work is what compacts well is my reading; neither source tests it.

title: A Finite State of Mind
text:
What would prove me wrong

Long context wins at equal cost. If, by the end of 2027, full-history agents beat compacted ones by more than a few points at the same serving cost.
Compaction works without checks. If written-state agents match full history on open-ended work with no verifiable end, my link between checkability and compaction is wrong.
Bench sciences catch up without labs. If AI use per researcher in chemistry and biomedicine matches the formal sciences before lab automation spreads.


Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.
Follow new posts. Subscribe to the newsletter on LinkedIn, or to the RSS feed. The archive lists recent changes.


Read next · Where Memory Lives Four experiments on what a small model should remember and what it should look up, including when the KV cache outweighs the model.


The views in this analysis are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
text:
Position paper, November 2026. Provocative by intention. The thesis is stated more sharply than the evidence can yet prove, to start an argument. It is not a warning against AI coding; it challenges how we use it. It is written for product and platform software; safety-critical software, where certification requires human review, is outside its scope. It follows Stop Reviewing Pull Requests and Review the Intent, Not the Diff. Figures 1 to 3 come from the simulations in sim.py (numbers in results.json); Figures 4 and 5 are schematics of my own.
Abstract. AI agents now fix most real-world issues in the standard benchmark, and write a large share of new code at major companies. Yet the default control is unchanged: a person reads every change. I argue this puts people in the wrong place. Generated code is chaotic: small differences in prompt or context give very different programs. That is mostly harmless. Stability comes from an attractor, checks that pull behaviour back to the promise after every change, not from a predictable path. Machines should run that loop everywhere, with one condition: the checks are protected from the agents they check. People gate only what cannot be undone, and otherwise move above the loop: they set the promise, own the checks, structure the system and choose the direction.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
section: 1. A remarkable year, an unchanged habit
text:
1. A remarkable year, an unchanged habit
What the last year achieved:

Agents solve real issues. On SWE-bench Verified (500 real GitHub issues), the best model resolved 33.2% in August 2024 (OpenAI 2024) and 80.9% in November 2025 (Anthropic 2025).
AI writes production code. More than a quarter of new code at Google was AI-generated by late 2024 (Pichai 2024).
Adoption is the norm. 84% of developers use or plan to use AI tools (Stack Overflow 2025).

What did not change: Google’s sentence continues, the code is “then reviewed and accepted by engineers” (Pichai 2024). That is the industry default. We built a generator that writes in minutes what took a team days, and kept a person at its output reading every line. Trust is low (46% of developers distrust AI accuracy, 33% trust it (Stack Overflow 2025)), and the usual answer to distrust is more reading.
The provocation:

Stop reading every line your AI writes. Automate the loop, gate a sliver, and move people above it.

The usual objection is one word: chaos. Generated code is not repeatable. The same coding task, sent several times to the same model, often returns programs that behave differently, even at temperature zero (Ouyang et al. 2023); even “deterministic” serving varies with how requests are batched (He and Thinking Machines Lab 2025). This paper takes chaos literally, and argues it is good news.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
text:
2. What the evidence says
Asked where do things go wrong?, the research since 2021 is consistent:

The field already judges behaviour, not code. HumanEval scores programs by passing tests (pass@k), not by similarity to a reference (Chen et al. 2021); SWE-bench counts a patch if the repository’s tests pass (Jimenez et al. 2024). The progress above is progress measured by checks.
Weak tests hide wrong code. Adding more tests to HumanEval cut pass rates by 19 to 29% across 26 models (Liu et al. 2023). The code did not change; the checking did.
Security fails where nothing checks. About 40% of Copilot programs in security-relevant scenarios had a known weakness (Pearce et al. 2022). Assistant users wrote less secure code and felt more confident (Perry et al. 2023). Models suggest non-existent packages (at least 5.2% for commercial models, 21.7% for open ones) that attackers can register (Spracklen et al. 2025).
Speed and stability are mixed. Copilot users were 55.8% faster on a controlled task (Peng et al. 2023); experienced developers on mature projects were 19% slower while feeling faster (Becker et al. 2025). DORA linked more AI adoption to 7.2% lower delivery stability, likely through larger changes (DORA 2024). Copy-pasted code is rising and refactoring falling (GitClear 2025).
Checks can be generated. Meta’s TestGen-LLM extended test suites; 73% of its filtered proposals were accepted for production (Alshahwan et al. 2024).

Where these failures sit becomes clear once the three zones are defined; Table 2, in the next section, classifies each finding.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
text:
3. The picture: an attractor
Lorenz showed in 1963 that a simple deterministic weather model cannot be predicted for long (Lorenz 1963). The other half of his lesson matters more here: every unpredictable run lives on the same shape, the attractor, and the model’s climate is stable (Strogatz 2015) (Figure 1). Netflix’s chaos engineering applies the same idea to software: inject failures on purpose, and judge the system only by whether a steady state holds (Basiri et al. 2016).



Figure 1. The Lorenz system, run twice from starting points 10^{-8} apart. Top: the paths part after about t \approx 18. Bottom: both trace the same butterfly, with the same long-run average (23.6 and 23.4). Unpredictable path, predictable place. Computed by sim.py.


For generated code, the picture gives three zones:

Table 1. Three zones of freedom in generated code.







Zone
What it is
Examples




1. Held
Behaviour the checks verify; pulled back on every change. The attractor.
Tests, types, contracts, scanners, budgets


2. Free, harmless
What nobody can observe from outside.
Names, structure, order of lines, which equivalent algorithm


3. Free, not yet harmless
Observable behaviour no check holds yet. It drifts with the code.
Security properties, latency, edge cases, what users rely on



Controlling zone 2 buys almost no stability. Moving zone 3 into zone 1 buys almost all of it. Both are work machines can do on every change, faster than any reviewer.
The evidence, zone by zone. None of the studies in Section 2 classifies failures this way, so Table 2 is my classification, stated so that it can be disputed. Prediction P2 tests it.

Table 2. The evidence of Section 2, classified by zone (my classification).








Finding
What actually failed
Zone
What holds it




Wrong programs passed weak tests (Liu et al. 2023)
Behaviour nobody checked
3 · unchecked
More tests, property-based tests


Known weaknesses in generated code (Pearce et al. 2022)

3 · unchecked
Static analysis, security tests in the session


Less secure code, more confidence (Perry et al. 2023)
Security unchecked; human reading did not catch it
3 · unchecked
The same checks; not more reading


Invented packages (Spracklen et al. 2025)

Package allowlist, provenance checks

1 · held, too slowly
Checks in the session, small changes

3 · unchecked
