The checks themselves
1 · held, under attack
Read-only and hidden checks



In no row is the failure the code being different from what a person would write, and in no row is the remedy “make the generator reproducible” or “read more carefully”. Every remedy is a check, a faster loop or a protected check.






NoteFor readers who like equations





Code is a state x; behaviour is a smaller observation y = \phi(x). Most directions of x change nothing in y (zone 2, the null space of \phi). If the agent pushes behaviour away at rate \lambda, and each check-and-fix cycle of length \Delta t removes a share \kappa of the error, checked behaviour holds when

-\frac{\ln(1-\kappa)}{\Delta t} \;>\; \lambda ,

the synchronisation condition for chaotic systems (Pecora and Carroll 1990). It rewards a high \kappa and a short \Delta t: an automated check in the agent’s session, not a slow human reading.









Where the analogy holds, and where it breaks. It holds on three points: small differences in input grow into large differences in code; the code stays bounded; and checks act like dissipation, pulling observed behaviour back. It also survives the fact that language models are partly random rather than chaotic: the theory of random dynamical systems extends attractors to systems driven by noise (Arnold 1998). It breaks on one point that matters: nature gave Lorenz his attractor, but a team must build its own. The climate is not discovered; it is the promise, and people decide it. That is why they belong above the loop.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
text:
4. A toy illustration
An illustration, not evidence: a chaotic toy agent (Sompolinsky et al. 1988) writes “code” of 300 numbers, “behaviour” is 30 numbers computed from it, and “tests” check some of the 30 and fix 80% of the error after each step. Two runs started 10^{-8} apart end with unrelated code, while tested behaviour stays about a hundred times closer and untested behaviour drifts with the code (Figure 2). At full coverage, behaviour error falls to 2.7% of the untested level while the code stays far apart, and across seven levels of chaos the error depends only on how firmly the loop corrects (Figure 3).



Figure 2. Two runs of the toy agent, same specification, starting 10^{-8} apart (log scale). Code (navy) parts completely; tested behaviour (green) stays about a hundred times closer; untested behaviour (amber) drifts with the code. Computed by sim.py.





Figure 3. (a) Behaviour error (navy) falls only as test coverage rises; the code of different runs (grey) stays far apart throughout. (b) Behaviour error against loop strength for seven levels of chaos: the curves overlap. Computed by sim.py.


The toy was built to show this picture, so it confirms only that the picture is coherent. The claim about real teams rests on Section 2 and on the predictions in Section 9.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
section: 5. Automate the zones, gate a sliver
text:
5. Automate the zones, gate a sliver



Figure 4. What to do with each zone. Zone 1: automate, strong and fast. Zone 2: leave to the machine. Zone 3: machines turn it into checks. People gate only the irreversible. Schematic, my own.



Zone 1, automated. Checks run in the agent’s session after every change; the agent reads failures and fixes them. Same checks, run sooner, hold more.
Zone 2, left to the machine. If some structure matters to someone (a size budget, a boundary, a forbidden dependency), it is observable and becomes a zone 1 check. Otherwise it is not a problem.
Zone 3, shrunk by machines.

Agents extend the tests, filtered as Meta did: they must build, pass reliably and add coverage (Alshahwan et al. 2024).
Mutation testing measures how firmly the checks hold (Petrović and Ivanković 2018); property-based tests hold whole families of behaviour (Claessen and Hughes 2000).
Regeneration drills: regenerate a module from its promise and checks, compare old and new on random inputs (differential testing (McKeeman 1998)); every disagreement is zone 3, and a missing check.
Real usage becomes contract tests, to keep up with Hyrum’s law: everything observable will be depended on (Winters et al. 2020).
A daily audit of the whole codebase, as in Stop Reviewing Pull Requests.

Protect the attractor. An attractor made of tests has one weakness: the generator can attack it. Frontier models have been seen editing tests or scoring code to pass (Von Arx et al. 2025). On versions of SWE-bench where the only way to pass is to break the specification, GPT-5 cheated in 54% of tasks; Claude models cheated mostly by editing the tests. Read-only tests stopped the edits but not other tricks such as special-casing; hiding the tests brought cheating near zero, at some cost in performance (Zhong et al. 2025). So the attractor has two layers: checks the agent can read but not change, run in its session; and held-out checks it never sees, run outside it, like a held-out test set. Agents may propose new or changed checks; a change that adds a check is merged by rule, a change that weakens or deletes one goes to a person.
A sliver, gated by people. Only actions whose harm survives a revert, decided at the point of no return. Approve what you cannot undo; watch everything else. The next subsection says what that means in practice.


A sliver, gated by people
What qualifies. One test: if this goes wrong, can a revert, a flag or a rollback restore the world as it was? If yes, no gate. If no, a gate. In practice the list is short:

data deleted, migrated or overwritten without a copy;
money that moves, and messages that leave: emails, notifications, published documents;
releases to users where rollback is not instant, and changes to access rights;
new dependencies and new external services, which widen the supply chain;
any change that weakens or deletes a check (see Protect the attractor).

Where it sits. At the point of no return, not at the merge. Code merges when the checks pass; the gate fires when the irreversible act is about to happen: the migration runs, the payment leaves, the release starts. It guards the act, not the code.
What the person sees. Not a diff, but a short packet the machines prepare: what the action does, in the words of the promise; which checks passed, including the held-out ones; exactly what cannot be undone, and how much of it (rows, customers, amounts); and the rollback plan for everything else. The person answers three questions: is this the intended act, is its reach acceptable, and is now the right time?
Who decides. The owner of the module’s attractor, or someone they name, with a second person for the largest actions, such as a schema change on customer data. Rotating the role spreads knowledge of the system.
How it stays thin. Every gated action is also a question for the people above the loop: could it be made reversible? Soft deletes instead of deletes, copies before migrations, feature flags and staged rollouts, dry runs, payments held for a review period. Each such change takes an action off the list. The measure is the share of changes that needed a person (Section 7). In the simulation of Stop Reviewing Pull Requests, a team merging 40 changes a day needed about 80 minutes of people time a day for the thin gate and the daily audit together, instead of 16 hours for reviewing everything.
What it is not. Not a code review, and not a signature on the code. The person at the gate is accountable for the act, as an operator is today when they press “run” on a migration.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
text:
6. People above the loop
Out of the loop is not out of the system. The human is still there, above the loop, guiding and structuring the whole. The level of the work changes, not its importance.



Figure 5. Where people work when the code is generated: above the loop, continuously; the loop itself is run by machines; people return at the gate only for what cannot be undone. Metrics, drills and incidents flow back up. Schematic, my own.


Above the loop, people:

Own the promise. Intent is the source; code is its output (Intent Is the Source). Understanding comes from the promise, not from diffs (Review the Intent, Not the Diff).
Own the checks. Not each test, which agents write, but what must always hold: properties, boundaries, budgets, security rules. They accept or refuse any change that would weaken a check.
Structure the system. Architecture and dependencies are the shape of the attractor; once decided, they become checks.
Read the instruments. Escaped defects, mutation scores, loop times, drills, incidents. They change the system that produces code, not individual changes, as Fast AI argued: slow, careful work done once, so the fast path runs on its own.
Choose what to build and what to remove. Making is cheap; choosing is not (The Joy of the Question, Work Has Mass).

A person who reads a thousand lines a day guards a thousand lines. A person who makes “every endpoint has an authorisation test” a check guards every line every agent will ever write there.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
section: 7. What it means for a team
text:
7. What it means for a team
The team owns the promise, the checks and the gates, not the text of the code. If it cannot regenerate a module from these, it does not really own it.
An example. A team adds “export invoices as CSV”.

Promise (a person, above the loop): customers can export their own invoices for a date range; amounts match the ledger.
Required checks (a person decides, an agent writes them): for any date range, the exported total equals the ledger total; no other customer’s invoice ever appears; 10,000 invoices export in under two seconds; every file parses with a standard CSV reader.
The loop (machines): the agent writes the code and extra tests; the required checks are read-only to it, and two held-out cases run outside its session.
Zone 3, found by a machine: a regeneration drill disagrees with the first version on customer names that contain a comma. The agent proposes a round-trip check (export, parse, compare); it adds a check, so it merges by rule.
The gate: none. Exporting reads data and can be undone. If the feature also emailed the file to customers, sending would be gated.
The people’s time: writing the promise and four checks, and later reading one drill report. Nobody read the code.


Table 3. What changes for a team.






Stop
Start




Reading every generated diff as the default control
Promise and required checks before the agent builds


Demanding reproducible generation (He and Thinking Machines Lab 2025)
All checks inside the agent’s session


Style debates nobody depends on
Machines that find zone 3: mutation tests, drills, usage-based contracts, daily audit


Asking “who wrote this line?”
Asking “which check was missing?”


Counting lines reviewed
Budgets for size, duplication and coupling (GitClear 2025)



A short, written list of gates



Roles. Each module has an owner of its attractor: the promise, the required checks, the gates. Security and platform engineers own the shared checks every agent session runs. Nobody is accountable for reading every line.
Metrics.

Escaped defects, classified by zone (unchecked behaviour, or weak checks).
Mutation score: how firmly the checks hold.
Time from change to check result: how fast the loop pulls back.
Behaviour agreement between regenerations: how much of zone 3 is left.
Share of changes that needed a human gate: is it still a sliver?
Size, duplication and coupling trends: is the code gaining mass?

One test of the whole idea. Delete a module and regenerate it from its promise and checks. Would you ship it unread? If not, your reasons are the checks you are missing, and that list is the team’s real backlog.
Getting there. Building the attractor costs effort, and no team should drop review overnight. A sequence that keeps risk bounded:

Pick one module with good tests. Measure its mutation score, make its checks read-only to agents and run them in the session.
Write the gate list for it: the few actions that cannot be undone.
Run regeneration drills and add a check for every disagreement they find.
Lower review step by step (every change, then a sample, then only the gate) while escaped defects and recovery time hold. If they do not, the missing checks show where.
Repeat module by module. The share of changes that needs a person is the progress metric.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
section: 8. Security and the rest, in a nutshell
text:
8. Security and the rest, in a nutshell
Security is not an exception. It is the most important part of zone 3, and it is held the same way.

Table 4. Security and other concerns: almost all held by machines, a few gated, the rest decided above the loop.







Concern
How it is held
Who acts




Injection, unsafe APIs, known weaknesses (Pearce et al. 2022)
Static analysis and security linters in every session; security tests per entry point
Machines


Secrets
Secret scanning before anything leaves the session; no credentials in the agent’s reach
Machines


Supply chain (Spracklen et al. 2025)
Package and registry allowlists, lockfiles, provenance checks
Machines; a person approves a new dependency


Access control, privacy
Authorisation tests per endpoint; data-flow checks; policy as code
Machines; people set the policy


The agent itself
Sandboxed sessions; never private data, untrusted input and a way out at once (The Context Is the Wire)
Machines enforce; people set the rule


Gaming the checks (Von Arx et al. 2025; Zhong et al. 2025)
Read-only checks in the session; hidden held-out checks outside it; weakening or deleting a check needs a person
Machines enforce; people approve


Irreversible actions
Data deletion, payments, releases
A person, at the gate


Performance, cost
Latency, memory and cost budgets, checked like tests
Machines; people set budgets


Maintainability
Size, duplication and coupling budgets; architecture rules as tests
Machines; people set the structure


Accessibility, licences, compliance
Automated checks and scanners; rules as code
Machines; people sample where automation is weak


Taste, fairness, product sense
Judgement on the promise and the product
People, above the loop



None of these depends on someone reading code; human review missed them before AI too, and assistant users grew more confident, not more careful (Perry et al. 2023). A rule turned into a check protects every future change; a careful reading protects one.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
text:
9. Predictions and a test protocol
Each prediction names what would refute it.

P1. Regeneration. Regenerated code differs widely; behaviour agrees on the checks and diverges elsewhere in proportion to what is unchecked. Refuted if code similarity predicts correct behaviour better than coverage and mutation score.
P2. Failures. Escaped defects in AI-written code come mostly from zone 3 or weak checks, not from “strange-looking code”. Refuted if reviewers’ sense of unusual code predicts them better.
P3. Automation beats reading. Effort on automated checks, mutation testing and drills prevents more escaped defects than the same effort on reading diffs. Refuted if reading prevents at least as many.
P4. Fast loops. The same checks run in the agent’s session reduce defects and rework compared with later CI. Refuted if timing makes no difference.
P5. Teams. Teams that gate only the irreversible and work above the loop deliver at least as fast with no more incidents. Refuted if, in a stepped-wedge trial as in Stop Reviewing Pull Requests, they have more incidents or slower recovery.

Protocol. For P1, P3 and P4, a regeneration study: take modules with good tests, regenerate each twenty times under each condition (review or not, checks in session or in CI), and compare three distances: between the programs, on the checks, and on random inputs by differential testing (McKeeman 1998). For P2 and P5, a stepped-wedge trial: teams adopt the rule one at a time in random order, and escaped defects are classified by zone from incident reports, not from opinions about the code.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
text:
10. Objections, briefly

“Taking people out of the loop is reckless.” They leave the loop, not the system, and keep the gate for the irreversible. The reckless default is a slow, partial check on every change that does not reliably catch insecure code (Perry et al. 2023).
“This is randomness, not chaos.” The argument only needs small input differences to grow and the code to stay bounded; generated code does both at any temperature (Ouyang et al. 2023; He and Thinking Machines Lab 2025). The toy is deterministic on purpose: even perfect determinism would not restore control.
“The agents will game the checks.” They do when they can (Von Arx et al. 2025; Zhong et al. 2025). That is why the checks they see are read-only, the checks that decide are hidden from them, and any weakening of a check is a human decision. Reading diffs is a weaker defence: a test edited or special-cased to pass is easy to miss in a large change.
“Some behaviour cannot be checked.” True: for much behaviour there is no cheap oracle that says what the right answer is (Barr et al. 2015). Partial oracles help (properties, metamorphic relations, differential tests against the previous version). What still cannot be checked stays above the loop, as a decision on the promise, or goes through a slower path with a person, until a check can be written. The thesis is about the default, not about every line.
“Regulated software requires review.” Some does: airborne software certified under DO-178C, for example, requires reviews of the code (RTCA 2011). That is out of scope by design. Even there, automated checks can supply much of the evidence; the gate list is simply longer.
“Untested behaviour is the danger.” Yes; that is the thesis. It shows up when code runs, not when it is read, so machines that run code differently find it, and a check holds it.
“Everything observable becomes depended on.” Hyrum’s law grows zone 3 over time (Winters et al. 2020). That cost exists for hand-written code too, and automation pays it best.
“People must still read code.” Sometimes: incidents, audits, domains without checks. Reading stays allowed; it stops being the default control.
“Regenerations share blind spots.” They do (Knight and Leveson 1986). The claim is not redundancy, but that their differences are mostly harmless.
“Checks can be wrong.” An attractor is not a truth. That is why people belong above the loop, deciding what must hold, not inside it.
“The evidence is mixed.” As expected from teams that adopted a chaotic generator but kept the old control (Peng et al. 2023; Becker et al. 2025; DORA 2024). P5 is the test.

title: Let the Code Be Chaotic
text:
11. Conclusion
The last year proved machines can write working code. It has not yet changed where people stand while they do: at the output, reading.
Generated code is weather; the promised behaviour is climate. People do not need to forecast every gust. They decide the climate, build the instruments that keep it, and step in only where harm cannot be undone.
Automate the loop, gate a sliver, and move people above it. Let the code be chaotic: most of the chaos was never where the risk was.

Questions or objections? Reply under the newsletter edition on LinkedIn, or send me a message. Good questions often become the next essay.
